| Supervised fine tuning (SFT) | tens of thousands of prompt and ideal response pairs | next token prediction on that data | SFT model |
| Reward modelling | comparisons: rankings of several completions | classify which completion is better | reward model |
| Reinforcement learning (RL) | large set of prompts | maximise the reward model's score | RLHF model |

The talk's diagram is not to scale: pretraining is about 99 percent of the training compute, and the three fine tuning stages need far fewer GPUs for hours or days. Karpathy stresses that the recipe is new and fast changing (mid 2023). ChatGPT is an RLHF model. Models like Vicuna 13B are SFT models.
say: There are four stages that follow each other: pretraining, supervised fine tuning, reward modelling, and reinforcement learning. Each has its own dataset, its own objective, and produces a model. Pretraining is the big one, around ninety nine percent of the compute, with internet scale data, thousands of GPUs and potentially months of training. The other three are fine tuning stages that use few GPUs for hours or days. Together the last three turn a document completer into an assistant, and ChatGPT is a model that went through all four.
must_mention: pretraining, SFT, reward modelling, reinforcement learning
each stage has data, objective and a model
pretraining is about 99 percent of compute

followups.q: Which stages produce a model you could deploy as an assistant?
followups.a: SFT and RLHF models. The base model is a document completer and the reward model only scores answers.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: What goes into pretraining data, and what is tokenization for?
plain: Pretraining data is a mixture of many text sources, mixed in fixed proportions. In the LLaMA paper, the mixture includes web crawls such as CommonCrawl and C4. It also has higher quality sources like GitHub, Wikipedia, books, arXiv and Stack Exchange. Documents are sampled according to the chosen proportions. Then the text is tokenised, meaning it is turned into integers, because generative pretrained transformer (GPT) models work on integers. The translation is lossless. A common method is byte pair encoding, which repeatedly merges common chunks of text into tokens.
deep:
Data mixture (from Meta's LLaMA paper): web scrapes (CommonCrawl, C4, which is also derived from CommonCrawl), plus curated sources such as GitHub, Wikipedia, books, arXiv and Stack Exchange. Sources are sampled according to given proportions to form the training set.

Tokenization is a lossless translation between raw text and sequences of integers, the native representation of a GPT. Typical algorithm: byte pair encoding, which iteratively merges frequent chunks of text into tokens. The integer sequence is what feeds the transformer. (The tokenizer is built from scratch in the later lecture on the GPT tokenizer.)

Hyperparameters of this stage: a vocabulary of a couple of tens of thousands of tokens, and a context length of 2,000 or 4,000, or in 2023 up to 100,000 tokens.
say: Pretraining data is a mixture of sources sampled in fixed proportions. In the LLaMA paper that means web crawls like CommonCrawl and C4, plus higher quality data like GitHub, Wikipedia, books, arXiv and Stack Exchange. Before training, all the text is tokenised, translated losslessly into sequences of integers, since that's the native representation GPTs work on. A common algorithm is byte pair encoding, which iteratively merges frequent chunks of text into tokens. The vocabulary is typically a few tens of thousands of tokens.
must_mention: mixture of web crawls and curated sources
tokenization is lossless text to integers

followups.q: Is tokenization lossy?
followups.a: No, it is a lossless translation between text and integers.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: Compare LLaMA and GPT-3 pretraining numbers. What does this say about parameters versus power?
plain: Parameter count does not decide how powerful a model is. LLaMA has 65 billion parameters, while GPT-3 has 175 billion. Yet LLaMA is more powerful, because it was trained much longer. GPT-3 is an older generative pretrained transformer model from OpenAI. It saw 1.4 trillion tokens, against 300 billion for GPT-3. That is about 21 tokens per parameter, against about 1.7. Training the 65 billion model took about 2,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), roughly 21 days, and several million dollars.
deep:
| Model | Parameters | Training tokens | Tokens per parameter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GPT-3 | 175 billion | 300 billion | about 1.7 |
| LLaMA 65B | 65 billion | 1.4 trillion | about 21.5 |

```python
print(round(1.4e12 / 65e9, 1), round(300e9 / 175e9, 2))   # 21.5 1.71
```

Karpathy: do not judge a model's power by its parameter count. The talk uses GPT-3's numbers because OpenAI released little detail about GPT-4. Other orders of magnitude from the slides: context length 2,000 to 4,000 tokens (or 100,000 nowadays), and for the 65B model Meta used 2,000 GPUs for roughly 21 days, a cost of several million dollars. The transformer's own hyperparameters are the number of heads, the width and the number of layers.
say: Parameter count doesn't determine power. LLaMA has sixty five billion parameters, much less than GPT-3's hundred seventy five billion, but it's significantly more powerful because it was trained for much longer, on one point four trillion tokens instead of three hundred billion. That's about twenty one tokens per parameter against less than two. Meta trained the sixty five billion model on about two thousand GPUs for roughly twenty one days, costing several million dollars. So I shouldn't judge a model by its size alone, the amount of training data matters too.
must_mention: do not judge power by parameter count

followups.q: Why use GPT-3 numbers in the talk?
followups.a: OpenAI released little information about how GPT-4 was trained.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: How does a pretraining batch look, and what does each position learn to predict?
plain: A pretraining batch is a grid of token integers, with batch size B rows and T columns, where T is the context length. Documents are packed into the rows, one after another. A special end of text token separates documents, telling the model where a new one starts. Every cell in the grid is a prediction task. The model reads all the tokens before that cell and predicts the next token. For example, with a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens, each cell gets 50,257 probabilities, and the true next token supplies the training signal.
deep:
Layout: an integer array of shape $(B,T)$, with $B$ independent rows and $T$ the maximum context length (2,000, 4,000 or more in practice). Documents are concatenated and separated by an end of text token.

For each cell, the transformer reads all earlier tokens in its row and outputs a distribution over the vocabulary (50,257 numbers for GPT-2 style vocabularies). The true next token, for example token 513, is the supervision. The loss is the usual negative log likelihood, applied at every cell in parallel, and batches are swapped continually.

Sampling from the trained model: predict, sample, append, repeat. A training run shows loss falling over time. Samples from a small GPT trained on Shakespeare go from random characters at initialisation to words, spaces and punctuation, with each improvement of the loss giving more coherent text. Transformers have tens of billions of parameters in practice.
say: A pretraining batch is a B by T array of token integers, B independent rows and T the context length. Documents are packed into the rows one after another with a special end of text token between them, so the model knows where a new document begins. Every cell is its own prediction task: the transformer reads all the tokens before that cell in the row and predicts the next one, as a distribution over, for example, fifty thousand tokens. The actual next token provides the supervision, and I apply the loss in parallel at every cell, batch after batch.
must_mention: B by T grid of tokens
documents packed with end of text tokens
each cell predicts the next token
loss applied at all cells in parallel

followups.q: What does the end of text token do?
followups.a: It marks where one document ends and another begins inside a packed row.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: How do base models relate to fine tuning and to prompting, and why is a base model not an assistant?
plain: A base model completes documents, so it answers a question with more questions. It does not try to be an assistant. During language modelling it learns general knowledge, so it can be fine tuned on a few examples for tasks like sentiment classification. That was the era of generative pretrained transformer 1 (GPT-1). By GPT-2, people found prompting works even better. In a few shot prompt you write fake document with example questions and answers. The model then continues with an answer to your question. For example, a prompt that starts with here is a poem about bread and cheese makes a base model write the poem.
deep:
Evolution described in the talk:

- Before: collect positive and negative examples, train a specialist model for each task.
- GPT-1: pretrain on language modelling, then fine tune efficiently with few examples. Works because predicting the next token forces the model to multitask over many concepts and structures in text.
- GPT-2: prompting beats fine tuning. Arrange a fake document, such as a passage followed by several question and answer pairs and then a new question (few shot prompting), and the model completes it with an answer. This kicked off the era of prompt engineering, with no training at all.

Base models are not assistants. Given a request they continue the document, perhaps with more questions. A prompt such as here is a poem about bread and cheese works better. You can even trick a base model into assistant behaviour with a few shot dialogue prompt, but it is not reliable.

Availability then: GPT-4's base model was not released, the GPT-3 base model was available through the API (davinci), GPT-2 weights were published, and LLaMA was the best open base model, though not commercially licensed.
say: A base model just completes documents, so if I ask it a question it may reply with more questions. It isn't an assistant. During pretraining it learns powerful general representations, so it can be fine tuned efficiently with a few examples for a specific task, like sentiment classification. Around GPT-2, people found prompting works even better: I arrange a fake document, like several question and answer pairs followed by my question, and the model completes it with an answer. That is few shot prompting. I can even trick a base model into acting like an assistant, but it's not reliable.
must_mention: fine tuning on few examples works
few shot prompting arranges a fake document
base model is not an assistant

followups.q: Why does fine tuning a pretrained model work so well?
followups.a: Next token prediction forces the model to learn the structure and many concepts in text, which transfer to downstream tasks.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: What is supervised fine tuning, and what does the data look like?
plain: Supervised fine tuning (SFT) continues training the base model on a small, high quality set of prompts and ideal answers. Human contractors write these prompt and response pairs, typically tens of thousands of them, such as 20,000. The algorithm does not change: it is still language modelling, predicting the next token. Only the training set changes, from huge amounts of internet text to a small amount of curated data. Contractors follow long labelling instructions and aim for helpful, truthful and harmless answers. The result is an SFT model, and it can be deployed as a working assistant.
deep:
Data: prompt and ideal response pairs written by human contractors, tens of thousands of examples. Example prompt: write a short introduction about the relevance of the term monopsony; the contractor writes the ideal response.

Objective: unchanged language modelling (next token prediction), but trained on low quantity, high quality data instead of high quantity, low quality internet documents.

Contractors follow extensive labelling documents asking for helpful, truthful and harmless responses. After training you get an SFT model, which can be deployed and works as an assistant to some extent. Examples of SFT models mentioned: Vicuna 13B and Koala. Later in the talk SFT is described as achievable, because it is just a continuation of the language modelling task and is relatively straightforward.
say: In supervised fine tuning, I collect a small but high quality dataset of prompts and ideal responses, written by human contractors, typically tens of thousands of examples. The algorithm doesn't change at all, it's still language modelling, I just swap the training set from internet documents to this curated prompt and response data, so it's low quantity and high quality. The contractors follow detailed labelling instructions to be helpful, truthful and harmless. The result is an SFT model, which already works as an assistant to some extent, and it's relatively straightforward to achieve.
must_mention: prompt and ideal response pairs from contractors

followups.q: What changes compared with pretraining?
followups.a: Only the dataset: small, high quality assistant data replaces huge internet text.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: How is a reward model trained from human comparisons?
plain: A reward model is a network that scores how good an answer is, and it is trained from human rankings. Take one prompt and have the supervised fine tuning (SFT) model write several answers, say 3. People rank the answers from best to worst. That gives pairs: with 3 answers there are 3 pairs. Each answer goes into the transformer with a special reward token at the end. The score is read from that token only. The loss pushes the better answer to score higher than the worse one in each pair. Ranking can take people hours for a single prompt.
deep:
Data: comparisons. For each prompt, sample several completions from the SFT model and have humans rank them. All pairs of completions become binary classification examples (which one is better).

Model: lay out the prompt and one completion in a row and append a special reward readout token. Supervise the transformer only at that token, where it outputs a scalar reward. The standard pairwise loss (as in the InstructGPT paper, a standard fact not spelled out in the talk) is $-\log\sigma(r_{\text{better}}-r_{\text{worse}})$.

```python
import math
def pair_loss(r_better, r_worse):
    return math.log1p(math.exp(-(r_better - r_worse)))
print(round(pair_loss(1.0, -1.2), 3), round(pair_loss(-1.2, 1.0), 3))   # 0.105 2.305
```

Reward predictions consistent with the ranking give low loss. The result scores any completion for any prompt. It is not useful as an assistant by itself, but it powers the reinforcement learning stage. The talk's example prompt asks for a function that checks whether a string is a palindrome.
say: For the reward model, I switch the data to comparisons. I take a prompt, get the SFT model to write several completions, and have people rank them, which is hard and can take hours per prompt. Each ranking gives pairs of better and worse completions. I feed each completion to the transformer with a special reward token appended, and supervise only the output at that token, a single score. The loss makes the better completion score higher than the worse one. The result can score any answer, but it isn't an assistant, and it's used in the next stage.
must_mention: rank several SFT completions per prompt
pairs of better and worse answers
scores answers, not an assistant itself

followups.q: How many pairs do 3 ranked completions give?
followups.a: Three: best versus middle, best versus worst, middle versus worst.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: How does the reinforcement learning stage use the reward model?
plain: In the reinforcement learning stage, the model writes completions and the reward model scores them. The model starts as the supervised fine tuning (SFT) model. For each prompt it samples a completion. The reward model, now frozen, reads off a score. Then the usual language modelling loss is applied to the sampled tokens, weighted by that score. A high score, say plus 1.5, makes every sampled token in that row more likely in future. A negative score, like minus 1.2, makes those tokens less likely. Repeated over many prompts, the model learns to produce completions the reward model rates highly.
deep:
Procedure: take a large collection of prompts. For each, sample completions from the model being trained (initialised from the SFT model), append the reward token, and read the reward from the reward model, which is kept fixed. Apply the language modelling loss to the sampled (yellow) tokens, weighted by the reward.

- High reward (the example row scored well): all sampled tokens are reinforced, getting higher probability in the future.
- Negative reward (-1.2 in the example): the tokens sampled in that row are pushed down.

Doing this over many prompts and batches yields a policy whose completions score highly under the reward model. This is the RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) pipeline, and ChatGPT is an RLHF model. The method used in practice by OpenAI is PPO, as mentioned in the earlier lecture. Note: the transcript of the talk reads as if the negative case also gets a slightly higher probability, which is a speech slip, since the intent is that low reward lowers it.
say: In the reinforcement learning stage, I take the model I'm training, initialised from the SFT model, and sample completions for lots of prompts. The reward model, which is now fixed, scores each completion. Then I apply the usual language modelling loss to the tokens I sampled, but weighted by the reward. If a completion scored high, all its tokens become more likely in the future, and if it scored negative, say minus one point two, they become less likely. Over many batches the policy produces completions that the reward model rates highly. That's the RLHF pipeline.
must_mention: sample completions from the SFT initialised model
reward model is frozen and scores them
language modelling loss weighted by reward

followups.q: Why keep the reward model fixed?
followups.a: It is the fixed yardstick. If it kept changing, the policy would be chasing a moving target.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: Why might RLHF work better than supervised fine tuning, and what does it cost?
plain: Models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) are preferred by human raters, and one reason may be that comparing is easier than writing. Ask a contractor to write a good haiku about paper clips and many will struggle. Show them a few haikus and they can easily say which is better. So rankings use human judgement more cheaply. The cost is diversity. RLHF models lose some entropy, so their outputs are more peaked and vary less. A base model is better when you want many varied items. For example, given 7 Pokemon names, a base model invents many more, diverse names.
deep:
Evidence: the InstructGPT paper found that people prefer outputs of PPO (RLHF) models over SFT models, and over base models prompted to act as assistants. In the Berkeley ranking (Elo ratings) of assistants at the time, GPT-4 was by far the best, followed by Claude and GPT-3.5, which were RLHF models, while the open models such as Vicuna and Koala were SFT models.

Why might it work? No consensus, but one proposal is the asymmetry between generating and discriminating: it is much easier to judge which haiku is better than to write a good one, so comparison data lets annotators contribute better judgement.

Cost: RLHF models lose entropy. They give more peaked results and less variation than the base model, which has lots of entropy and diverse outputs. Karpathy still prefers a base model for tasks like generating more items similar to a list (cool Pokemon names from 7 examples).
say: RLHF models are preferred by people in evaluations, and one proposed reason is that comparing is much easier than generating. If I ask a contractor to write a great haiku about paper clips, they might not be good at it, but if I show them several haikus, they can easily judge which is better. So comparison data uses human judgement more effectively. The cost is that RLHF models lose some entropy, so their outputs are more peaked and less varied. For tasks like generating more items similar to a list, such as Pokemon names, I still prefer a base model.
must_mention: base model better for diverse generation

followups.q: What is entropy loss in this context?
followups.a: The outputs become more peaked, so repeated samples vary less than from a base model.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: Why do language models need tokens to think, and what does that imply for prompting?
plain: A language model spends the same amount of computation on every token, so it cannot do much reasoning in one token. A human writing a sentence has an inner monologue. They look things up, check numbers and rewrite. In the talk's example, a person works out that California's population is about 53 times Alaska's, using a calculator for 39.2 divided by 0.74. A generative pretrained transformer (GPT) just produces tokens one after another, with about 80 layers of work for each token. It does not reflect or check. So you should spread reasoning over many tokens, for example by asking it to think step by step.
deep:
Human writing the sentence California's population is 53 times that of Alaska: look up both populations (self knowledge of what is not known, tool use), use a calculator for $39.2/0.74\approx53$, sanity check the result, draft, delete awkward phrasing and retry. All that inner dialogue is stripped from the training data.

A GPT sees a sequence of tokens and spends the same compute on each (a transformer has about 80 layers, which is not much depth). It is a token simulator: it does not know what it does not know, does not reflect, check or recover from mistakes by default, and has no separate inner monologue.

Its cognitive advantages: vast factual knowledge (tens of billions of parameters), and a large, near perfect working memory in the context window, accessed directly through self attention.

Consequence: reasoning must be spread over more tokens. Do not expect a hard question to be answered in one token: these transformers need tokens to think. Few shot prompts that show the work, or the instruction let us think step by step, put the model in a mode of showing its work, with less computation needed per token.
say: A language model does the same amount of computation for every token, so I can't expect it to do much reasoning in a single token. A person has an inner monologue, looks things up, uses a calculator, and sanity checks, but all that is stripped out of the training data. A GPT just samples tokens, with about eighty layers of work each, and doesn't reflect or correct itself by default. So I spread the reasoning over many tokens, either with a few shot prompt that shows the work, or by asking it to think step by step. Transformers need tokens to think.
must_mention: no inner monologue or self checking
few shot work shown or think step by step

followups.q: What are the advantages of an LLM over a human here?
followups.a: A huge store of facts in its parameters and a perfect working memory for everything in its context window.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: How do self consistency, self checking and tree search help language models reason?
plain: These techniques give a model a way to look back and try again, which it cannot do by default. A model can sample an unlucky token and go down a blind alley, with no way to recover. Self consistency samples several answers and keeps the most common one, by majority vote. Self checking asks the model whether it met the assignment, and a strong model often knows it did not. Tree of Thought keeps several partial answers, scores them and expands the good ones. Together these recreate System 2 (slow deliberate planning) on top of System 1 (fast automatic token sampling).
deep:
Problem: once a token is sampled, the model is stuck with it, and continues even if the sequence will not work out.

- Self consistency: sample multiple times, then select good samples or take a majority vote.
- Self checking: ask did you meet the assignment? For example a model asked for a poem that does not rhyme may produce one that rhymes, but a large model such as GPT-4 will say no when asked, and try again. Without being asked, it does not check by itself.
- Tree of Thought: maintain multiple completions for a prompt, score them along the way and keep the promising ones. This needs Python glue code (a tree search that decides which prompts to expand), so it is a symbiosis of code and prompts. An analogy is AlphaGo's Monte Carlo tree search layered on top of its imitation trained policy.
- ReAct: structure the answer as thought, action, observation rollouts, with tool use.
- AutoGPT: keeps a task list and recursively breaks tasks down. Karpathy found it inspiring but did not advise using it in practice.

Majority vote example:

```python
from collections import Counter
answers = ['53', '53', '45', '53', '52']
print(Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0])   # ('53', 3)
```

These recreate System 2 thinking.
say: A language model can sample an unlucky token and be stuck with it, going down a blind alley with no way to recover by default. So I give it ways to look back. Self consistency samples several answers and takes a majority vote. Self checking just asks the model whether it met the assignment, and a strong model often knows it didn't, but it won't check unless asked. Tree of Thought keeps multiple partial answers, scores them, and expands the promising ones, using Python code around the prompts. Together these recreate System Two, slow deliberate thinking, on top of fast token sampling.
must_mention: model is stuck with sampled tokens
ask the model to check its work
tree of thought with scoring and search

followups.q: Why is Tree of Thought more than a prompt?
followups.a: It needs code that keeps several prompts and runs a tree search over them.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: Why should you explicitly ask a language model for a high quality answer?
plain: Language models imitate, they do not try to succeed, so you have to ask for success. The training data covers a whole range of quality. For a physics question there may be a wrong student answer and a correct expert answer. The model can tell both apart, but by default it imitates all of it. So you should ask for the good one. In one study, one prompt beat plain let us think step by step. It was let us work this out step by step to be sure we have the right answer. You can say you are a leading expert, or pretend you have an intelligence quotient (IQ) of 120, but not 400, which may land you in science fiction text.
deep:
Training data contains the full spectrum of quality, and a language modelling objective teaches the model to imitate all of it. At test time you must request good performance.

Evidence in the talk (a paper comparing prompts): let us think step by step was powerful because it spreads reasoning over many tokens. Even better was let us work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer, which is like conditioning on getting the right answer. The model need not hedge probability mass over low quality solutions.

Practical advice: ask for a strong solution, for example you are a leading expert on this topic, pretend you have IQ 120. Do not ask for too much IQ. IQ 400 may be out of the data distribution, or in the distribution of science fiction, and the model starts to roleplay. There is probably a U shaped curve, so you must find the right amount.
say: Language models want to imitate, not to succeed. Their training data contains the whole spectrum of quality, like a wrong student solution next to an expert one, and the model learned to imitate all of it. So at test time I have to ask for good performance. In the study Karpathy cites, the best prompt was let's work this out step by step to be sure we have the right answer, which conditions on a correct answer. I can say you are a leading expert, or pretend you have an IQ of one twenty. But not IQ four hundred, which might push it into science fiction territory.
must_mention: training data has all quality levels
ask explicitly for a strong answer
be sure we have the right answer

followups.q: Why can too much claimed IQ hurt?
followups.a: It may be out of the data distribution or match science fiction text, so the model starts roleplaying.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: Why give a language model tools and retrieved context, and how does retrieval augmented generation work?
plain: Tools and retrieved documents make up for what a model cannot do or does not know. A model does not know what it is bad at, so you can tell it to use a calculator for large arithmetic. The context window is the model's working memory, and anything placed there is directly available. Retrieval augmented generation fills it with relevant material. Split documents into chunks and embed each chunk as a vector (a list of numbers that captures its meaning). For example, a 3,000 word document might become 10 chunks of 300 words. Store the vectors. At query time, fetch the closest chunks, put them into the prompt, and generate.
deep:
Tools: calculators, code interpreters and search. The model by default does not know what it is good or bad at, so you may need to say, in the prompt, that it is poor at mental arithmetic and should use the calculator, and spell out how to call it.

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG): the pendulum swung from retrieval only to memory only (LLMs), and RAG sits in between and works very well. The context window is working memory, so loading relevant information lets the model use it immediately.

Recipe: split relevant documents into chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, store the vectors in a vector store, then at test time embed the query, fetch relevant chunks and stuff them into the prompt before generating. LlamaIndex is an example connector. It is like looking up a textbook or library documentation instead of relying on memory.

```python
import numpy as np
docs = ["California has about 39.2 million people",
        "Alaska has about 0.74 million people",
        "Python lists are mutable"]
vocab = sorted({w for d in docs for w in d.lower().split()})
def embed(t):
    v = np.array([t.lower().split().count(w) for w in vocab], float)
    return v / (np.linalg.norm(v) + 1e-9)
sims = np.stack([embed(d) for d in docs]) @ embed("how many people live in alaska")
print(sims.round(2).tolist(), int(sims.argmax()))   # [0.29, 0.58, 0.0] 1
```
say: Tools and retrieval make up for what the model can't do or doesn't know. The model doesn't know what it's bad at, so I tell it to use a calculator for big arithmetic, and spell out how to call it. The context window is its working memory, so anything I put there is immediately accessible through self attention. In retrieval augmented generation, I split documents into chunks, embed them as vectors, and store them. At query time I embed the query, fetch the nearest chunks, stuff them into the prompt, and generate. It's like looking something up in documentation instead of relying on memory.
must_mention: model does not know what it is bad at
chunk, embed, store, retrieve, stuff into the prompt

followups.q: Why can retrieval beat the model's own memory?
followups.a: Retrieved text sits in the context window, which the model reads losslessly, while parametric memory is fuzzy.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: What are constraint prompting and parameter efficient fine tuning, and how hard are SFT and RLHF to run?
plain: Constraint prompting forces the model's output to follow a template, such as valid JSON (a text format for structured data). Tools like Microsoft's Guidance edit the token probabilities, so only allowed tokens can be picked and the model fills in the blanks. Fine tuning changes the model weights. Methods such as LoRA (low rank adaptation) train only small pieces of the model, which is much cheaper. For example, a fine tune might train only a small share of the weights, such as 1 percent. The rest stays frozen, so it can run in low precision. Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is achievable because it is still language modelling. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is unstable research territory, so do not roll your own.
deep:
Constraint prompting (for example Microsoft's Guidance): enforce a template such as JSON. The library intervenes on the token probabilities coming from the transformer, clamping disallowed tokens, so the model only fills in the blanks, and extra restrictions can be placed on each blank. This guarantees the output form.

Fine tuning changes weights and is becoming accessible because of recent techniques and libraries:

- LoRA (a parameter efficient method): only small, sparse pieces of the model are trained, and the rest stays clamped at the base model, which makes tuning much cheaper. Frozen parts can use very low precision inference, which adds efficiency.
- Open, high quality base models such as LLaMA (not commercially licensed at the time).

Difficulty: fine tuning is more technically involved, needs human data contractors or synthetic data pipelines, and slows the iteration cycle. SFT is relatively straightforward, since it continues language modelling. RLHF is very much research territory: unstable, hard to train, not beginner friendly, and likely to change quickly. Karpathy would not advise anyone to roll their own implementation.
say: Constraint prompting forces the output into a template, like valid JSON. Libraries such as Microsoft's Guidance do it by clamping the token probabilities, so the model only fills in the allowed blanks. Fine tuning changes the weights, and it's much more accessible now thanks to parameter efficient techniques like LoRA, which trains only small pieces of the model while the rest stays frozen, so it's cheaper and the frozen part can use low precision. Supervised fine tuning is achievable because it's still language modelling. RLHF is research territory, unstable and hard, so I wouldn't try to roll my own.
must_mention: constraint prompting clamps tokens to a template
LoRA trains small pieces, rest frozen

followups.q: Why can the frozen parts of a LoRA model use low precision?
followups.a: They are not updated by gradient descent, so they only need to be stored and used for inference.

topic: Zero to Hero V8: State of GPT
q: What workflow does the talk recommend for building an application on language models, and what are the limitations?
plain: Work in two steps: first get the best performance, then cut cost. For the best performance, use the strongest model, which was GPT-4 (the fourth generative pretrained transformer) at the time. Write detailed prompts, with context and instructions, as if briefing a contractor who cannot reply. Add retrieved information, few shot examples, tools, and chains with reflection. Only after prompting is exhausted should you look at fine tuning. To save money, try smaller models and shorter prompts. Models can be biased, make things up, reason badly, have knowledge cutoffs such as September 2021, and be hijacked by prompt injection (hidden instructions in the input). So use them in low stakes settings with human oversight.
deep:
Step 1, achieve top performance: use GPT-4, the most capable by far. Write detailed prompts with task context, relevant information and instructions, like briefing a contractor who cannot email back, but remember that an LLM lacks a human's inner monologue and cleverness, so cater to its psychology. Retrieve and add relevant context. Experiment with few shot examples (show, do not just tell), with tools and plug-ins that offload hard tasks, and with chains, reflection and multiple samples.

Step 2, optimise: try lower capacity models, shorter prompts, and, once prompt engineering is squeezed out, fine tuning (slower, more fragile; RLHF works somewhat better than SFT if you can get it to work).

Limitations: bias, fabricated information (hallucination), reasoning errors, struggles on entire classes of tasks, knowledge cutoffs (for example September 2021 for these models), and attacks such as prompt injection, jailbreaks and data poisoning.

Recommendation: low stakes applications, always with human oversight. Use them as a source of inspiration and suggestions, think copilots, not fully autonomous agents.
say: I'd work in two steps. First achieve top performance with the strongest available model, which was GPT-4, using detailed prompts like I'm briefing a contractor who can't email back, plus retrieved context, few shot examples, tools, and chains with reflection. Second, optimise cost with smaller models or shorter prompts, and only after prompting is exhausted consider fine tuning. And I'd keep the limitations in mind: models can be biased, hallucinate, make reasoning errors, have knowledge cutoffs, and be attacked by prompt injection. So I'd use them in low stakes settings with human oversight, as copilots, not autonomous agents.
must_mention: detailed prompts, few shot, tools, retrieval
fine tuning only after prompting is exhausted

followups.q: What is prompt injection?
followups.a: An attack where untrusted text in the input contains instructions that hijack the model's behaviour.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: What is tokenization, and which model behaviours does it explain?
plain: Tokenization turns text into a list of integers, and turns integers back into text. A token is a chunk of text, and it is the basic unit a language model reads. Many odd model behaviours come from this step, not from the network. Models are weak at spelling, because one token can hold many letters. They do worse in languages other than English, because those split into more tokens. Numbers split in arbitrary ways, which hurts arithmetic. For example, an early model, generative pretrained transformer 2 (GPT-2), spent one token on each space in Python code.
deep:
A tokenizer is a translation layer between strings and sequences of tokens (integers), with `encode` and `decode`. Tokens are the atoms of an LLM: the context length (1,024 tokens for GPT-2) and the cost are counted in tokens, and the Llama 2 paper trained on 2 trillion tokens.

Problems that trace to tokenization, listed at the start of the lecture:

- poor spelling and other simple string processing
- worse performance in non English languages
- mistakes in simple arithmetic
- GPT-2's weakness at Python (wasted tokens on spaces)
- the trailing whitespace warning in completion APIs
- the strange behaviour on the string SolidGoldMagikarp
- why YAML is preferred over JSON for structured data (fewer tokens)

Karpathy's advice: do not brush it off. Issues that look like network problems are often tokenization problems. The earlier GPT lecture used only a naive character tokenizer, with 65 symbols and an embedding table of 65 rows.
say: Tokenization is the step that turns text into a sequence of integers, tokens, and back again. Tokens are the atoms of a language model, so the context length and the cost are all counted in them. A lot of strange behaviour that looks like a network problem actually traces back to this step. Spelling is weak because a token can hide many letters, other languages do worse because they split into more tokens, arithmetic suffers because numbers split arbitrarily, and GPT-2 was poor at Python because indentation wasted tokens. So I don't brush tokenization off.
must_mention: tokens are the atoms of LLMs
many issues blamed on the network are tokenization

followups.q: What did the previous GPT lecture use?
followups.a: A naive character level tokenizer with 65 symbols, not the subword schemes used in practice.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How do tokens depend on case, spaces and digits? Give examples from the Tiktokenizer app.
plain: The same word can become different tokens depending on case, spacing and position. In the tokenizer of generative pretrained transformer 2 (GPT-2), egg at the start of a sentence is 2 tokens. But space egg, with a leading space, is a single token. Lowercase egg is another single token with a different id, and capital Egg differs again. So one idea gets several unrelated ids, and the model must learn they are alike. Numbers split arbitrarily too. The number 127 is one token, while 677 is two.
deep:
Observations in the Tiktokenizer web app (GPT-2 tokenizer):

- The space is part of the token: the token for the word hello world's second word is space world, one chunk.
- `127 + 677`: 127 is one token, 677 is two. 804 is two tokens. Four digit numbers split as 1 and 3, 2 and 2, or 3 and 1, with no pattern.
- egg at the start of a sentence is 2 tokens, space egg is a single token, lowercase egg is a single, different token, and capital Egg is yet another. The tokenizer is case sensitive.

The language model must learn from the training text that all of these are almost the same concept, spending parameters on it. Integer ids are arbitrary labels for chunks.

This arbitrariness is one cause of weak arithmetic and of odd sensitivity to formatting, and it motivates the later discussion of the GPT-4 changes.
say: The tokenizer splits text by chunks it learned, so small changes in case, spacing or position change the tokens. In the GPT-2 tokenizer, egg at the start of a sentence is two tokens, but space egg with a leading space is one token, lowercase egg is another single token with a different id, and capital Egg is different again. The model has to learn from data that these are the same concept. Numbers behave arbitrarily too: one twenty seven is one token, six seventy seven is two, and four digit numbers split in no consistent way.
must_mention: leading space is part of the token
model must learn the equivalence from data

followups.q: Why is that a burden for the model?
followups.a: It must spend parameters and data learning that several different ids mean nearly the same thing.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: Why do language models work worse in non English languages, from a tokenization view?
plain: Text in other languages needs many more tokens for the same meaning, which wastes context. The tokenizer is trained on text that is mostly English. So English words get long merged tokens, while other languages are cut into small pieces. For example, hello how are you is 5 tokens, but its Korean translation is 15. That is 3 times as many. The longer sequence uses up the limited context sooner. The model also sees less non English data in training.
deep:
Causes: (1) the language model sees less non English text during training, and (2) the tokenizer's own training set has much more English, so it creates longer tokens for English and many small chunks for other scripts.

Effect: the token count for the same content is larger. Example from the lecture: hello how are you is 5 tokens and its Korean translation is 15, a $3\times$ blow up. The Korean greeting is 3 tokens, whereas the English hello is a single token.

Consequences: sequences are bloated, and in attention the tokens run out of the finite context length, so non English text is stretched from the transformer's perspective, and each token carries less information.

Mitigation: put more non English text (and the mix of code) in the tokenizer's training set, so that more merges are spent on those scripts and their sequences shrink. More Japanese text in the tokenizer's training data gives shorter Japanese sequences.
say: Non English text needs more tokens for the same content, so it eats up the limited context and each token carries less information. That's because the tokenizer is trained on mostly English text, so English gets long merged tokens and other scripts get chopped into small pieces. In the example from the lecture, hello how are you is five tokens, and its translation is fifteen, a three times blow up. On top of that, the model itself saw less non English data in training. The fix is to include more of those languages in the tokenizer's training set, so they get more merges.
must_mention: more tokens for the same meaning
fix: more non English data for the tokenizer

followups.q: How could a tokenizer be improved for Japanese?
followups.a: Add more Japanese text to its training set, so more Japanese merges are learned and sequences get shorter.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How do the GPT-2 and GPT-4 tokenizers compare, and what limits vocabulary growth?
plain: The tokenizer of generative pretrained transformer 4 (GPT-4) has about twice the vocabulary of generative pretrained transformer 2 (GPT-2). So it uses about half the tokens for the same text. GPT-2 has about 50,000 tokens, and GPT-4 has about 100,000. The lecture's sample text takes 300 tokens in GPT-2 and 185 in GPT-4. So the model sees about twice as much text in its context. GPT-4 also groups Python indentation spaces into single tokens. A bigger vocabulary is not always better, because the embedding table and output layer grow with it.
deep:
| Tokenizer | Vocabulary | Tokens for the lecture's sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPT-2 | about 50,000 | 300 |
| GPT-4 (cl100k_base) | about 100,000 | 185 |

The same text is squished into roughly half the tokens, a denser input. With a fixed context length, the transformer can attend to about twice as much text. In Python, GPT-2 spends one token (id 220) on every space of the indentation, which wastes context. GPT-4 groups runs of spaces (four spaces, or seven) into single tokens, a deliberate design choice by OpenAI. Karpathy concludes the improvement in coding ability from GPT-2 to GPT-4 comes partly from the tokenizer, and not only from the model and optimisation.

Limit: a bigger vocabulary enlarges the embedding table and the softmax at the output, so there is a sweet spot.
say: The GPT-4 tokenizer has roughly double the vocabulary of GPT-2, about a hundred thousand tokens against fifty thousand, so the same text takes about half the tokens. The lecture's example went from three hundred tokens to one eighty five. That means the transformer sees about twice as much text in its fixed context window. GPT-4 also groups runs of spaces into single tokens, which makes Python much denser, so part of its better coding comes from the tokenizer. But a bigger vocabulary isn't free, because the embedding table and the output layer grow with it.
must_mention: 300 versus 185 tokens for the same text
twice as much text in context
bigger vocabulary grows embedding and output layers

followups.q: Why is more not always better for vocabulary size?
followups.a: The embedding table and the softmax grow, and rare tokens get too few training examples.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: What are Unicode code points, and why not feed them to the model directly?
plain: Unicode code points are numbers that name characters from all writing systems. Python strings are sequences of code points. The Unicode standard defines about 150,000 characters across 161 scripts. The ord function gives a character's code point. For example, h is 104, and a waving hand emoji is 128,075. We could feed these integers to a model with no tokenizer. But the vocabulary would have about 150,000 entries, and the standard keeps changing.
deep:
A Python string is an immutable sequence of Unicode code points. The Unicode standard (version 15.1 in September 2023) defines roughly 150,000 characters across 161 scripts. `ord(c)` gives the code point of a single character and `chr` is the inverse.

```python
print(ord('h'), ord('안'), ord('👋'), chr(104))   # 104 50504 128075 h
```

`ord` takes one character only, not a string.

Why not use the code points as tokens: (1) the vocabulary would be about 150,000 long, which makes the embedding table and output layer large and most entries rare, and (2) the standard is alive and keeps changing, so it is not a stable representation. So the lecture turns to encodings, which translate text into bytes.
say: Unicode code points are integers that name characters across all scripts. Python strings are sequences of them, and the standard defines roughly a hundred fifty thousand characters in a hundred sixty one scripts. I get one with ord, so h is one oh four, and an emoji can be over a hundred twenty thousand. I could use those integers as tokens directly, but the vocabulary would be around a hundred fifty thousand long, with most entries rare, and the standard keeps changing, so it isn't a stable representation. That's why I move to encodings into bytes.
must_mention: strings are sequences of code points

followups.q: Can ord take a whole string?
followups.a: No, it takes a single character and returns its integer code point.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: Compare UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32. Why does the lecture choose UTF-8?
plain: UTF-8 is the preferred way to turn text into bytes. UTF stands for Unicode transformation format, and each version turns code points into bytes. UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per character, so its length varies. UTF-32 uses exactly 4 bytes for every character, which is wasteful. UTF-16 and UTF-32 put many zero bytes around simple English letters. For example, the letter h is 1 byte in UTF-8, 2 in UTF-16, and 4 in UTF-32. Only UTF-8 matches the older ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) encoding, which helps it dominate the internet.
deep:
All three translate code points to byte streams: UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point (variable length), UTF-16 uses 2 or 4, UTF-32 is fixed length, 4 bytes.

```python
print(list("hello".encode('utf-8')))             # [104, 101, 108, 108, 111]
print(list("hi".encode('utf-16'))[:6])           # [255, 254, 104, 0, 105, 0], zeros between letters
print(len("hi".encode('utf-32')), list("안".encode('utf-8')))   # 12 [236, 149, 136]
```

For simple ASCII text, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are wasteful, with zeros after each byte of content. UTF-8 is backward compatible with ASCII, which is a major advantage, and the UTF-8 Everywhere manifesto argues it is a lot nicer, which is why it is used much more on the internet. UTF-32's advantage (fixed length) comes with many downsides.

In UTF-8 a multi byte character has a specific envelope of leading bits, which is why not every byte sequence is valid UTF-8 (see the decoding card).
say: UTF-8 turns each Unicode code point into one to four bytes, so it's variable length, and it's by far the most common. UTF-32 is fixed length, four bytes each, but wasteful, and UTF-16 also puts lots of zero bytes around simple English characters. UTF-8 is also the only one that is backward compatible with ASCII, which helps explain why it dominates on the internet. For our purposes I want compact bytes for ordinary text, so I stick with UTF-8, and then I use byte pair encoding on top of those bytes to compress them further.
must_mention: UTF-8 is 1 to 4 bytes, variable length
UTF-16 and UTF-32 waste zeros on English
UTF-8 is backward compatible with ASCII

followups.q: How many bytes is a Korean syllable in UTF-8?
followups.a: Three bytes in the example, such as 236, 149, 136.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: Why not feed raw UTF-8 bytes to the model, and what is the alternative?
plain: Raw bytes give a vocabulary of only 256, which makes every text very long. The embedding table (one learned vector per token) would be tiny. But sequences would be several times longer. Attention is expensive and the context length is finite, so the model could see much less text. For example, a paragraph of 533 characters becomes 616 bytes. So we want a larger vocabulary that we can tune. Byte pair encoding compresses byte sequences into shorter token sequences.
deep:
Raw UTF-8 bytes give vocabulary 256. The embedding table and the final softmax are tiny, but sequences are very long (in the lecture's paragraph, 533 code points become 616 bytes, and non ASCII characters take up to 4 bytes). With a finite context length and quadratically costly attention, long sequences mean we cannot attend to enough text for next token prediction.

So we keep the UTF-8 encoding but compress the byte sequences to a variable amount with byte pair encoding, giving a vocabulary size we can set as a hyperparameter.

Tokenization free alternative: a 2023 paper proposed a hierarchical transformer to feed raw bytes (they argued tokenization free autoregressive sequence modelling at scale is viable). Karpathy would love that, but it has not been proven out by enough groups at scale, and it requires modifying the transformer architecture, since attention becomes very expensive on very long sequences.
say: Raw bytes give a vocabulary of only two hundred fifty six, so the embedding table and the output layer are tiny, but every text becomes a very long sequence. Attention is expensive and the context length is finite, so the model could see much less text before the point it has to predict. So I want a bigger vocabulary I can tune, while keeping the UTF-8 bytes underneath, and byte pair encoding does that by compressing byte sequences. A tokenization free model would be wonderful, but it needs architectural changes and hasn't been proven at scale yet.
must_mention: tokenization free models not yet proven

followups.q: What would tokenization free modelling need?
followups.a: A modified, hierarchical transformer, because attention on raw byte sequences is too expensive.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How does the byte pair encoding algorithm work? Use a small example.
plain: Byte pair encoding repeatedly replaces the most common pair of neighbouring tokens with a new token. Start with a sequence over a small vocabulary. Count all adjacent pairs and pick the most frequent. Make a new token for it, replace every occurrence, and repeat. For example, aaabdaaabac has 11 symbols over a vocabulary of 4. Replace aa with Z to get 9 symbols and a vocabulary of 5. Replace ab with Y to get 7 symbols. Replace Z followed by Y with X to get 5 symbols.
say: Byte pair encoding repeatedly merges the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new token. Take aaabdaaabac, eleven symbols over a four symbol vocabulary. The pair aa is most frequent, so I mint a token Z for it and get nine symbols with a vocabulary of five. Then ab becomes Y, giving seven symbols, and Z followed by Y becomes X, giving five symbols and a vocabulary of seven. Each round shortens the sequence and grows the vocabulary by one. With real text I start from the two hundred fifty six bytes, and the merges I record let me encode and decode anything.
must_mention: find the most frequent adjacent pair
mint a new token and replace all occurrences
sequence shrinks, vocabulary grows by one

followups.q: Can a new token be merged again?
followups.a: Yes. New tokens are eligible in later rounds, as ZY became X in the example.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: Implement get_stats and merge for byte pair encoding.
plain: Two small functions do all the work of byte pair encoding. The first counts how often each neighbouring pair occurs, using a dictionary. The second walks the list and replaces every occurrence of a chosen pair with a new id. After a match, skip two positions. Also check that you are not on the last element, or you run off the end. For example, merging the pair 6, 7 into 99 turns 5, 6, 6, 7, 9, 1 into 5, 6, 99, 9, 1. In the lecture, the pair 101 then 32, which is the letter e then a space, occurred 20 times.
deep:
```python
def get_stats(ids):
    counts = {}
    for pair in zip(ids, ids[1:]):                 # consecutive pairs
        counts[pair] = counts.get(pair, 0) + 1
    return counts

def merge(ids, pair, new):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i < len(ids) - 1 and (ids[i], ids[i + 1]) == pair:   # guard against the last position
            out.append(new); i += 2                              # skip over the whole pair
        else:
            out.append(ids[i]); i += 1
    return out

print(merge([5, 6, 6, 7, 9, 1], (6, 7), 99))   # [5, 6, 99, 9, 1]
ids = list("the cat sat".encode('utf-8'))
stats = get_stats(ids)
top = max(stats, key=stats.get)
print(top, stats[top], chr(top[0]) + chr(top[1]))   # (97, 116) 2 at
```

The most common pair is found with `max(stats, key=stats.get)`. In the lecture on a blog post of 616 bytes, the top pair is (101, 32), the letters e and space, occurring 20 times, and merging it with id 256 takes the length from 616 to 596. New ids start at 256 because the raw byte tokens are 0 to 255. After the merge, no (101, 32) pair remains in the list, though 101 and 32 can still appear separately.
say: Two small functions. Get stats walks the list with zip of the list and its tail, and counts every consecutive pair in a dictionary. Merge takes the ids, a pair and a new id, and builds a new list: at each position, if the current element and the next one match the pair, I append the new id and skip two positions, otherwise I copy the element and move one. I have to guard against the last position so I don't read past the end. The top pair is the max of the stats by value, and new ids start at two fifty six, since the bytes occupy zero to two fifty five.
must_mention: max by count gives the top pair
skip two after a match, guard the last position

followups.q: How many tokens does a merge remove?
followups.a: One per occurrence of the pair, so the length drops by the pair's count: 616 to 596 for 20 occurrences.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How do you train a byte pair encoding tokenizer, and what is the vocabulary size?
plain: You train by repeating find and merge until the vocabulary reaches the size you chose. That size is a hyperparameter (a setting you choose before training). Start with the 256 bytes. Each merge adds one token, so the vocabulary size is 256 plus the number of merges. For example, 20 merges give a vocabulary of 276. Record each merge as a pair of child ids mapped to the new id. The compression ratio is bytes divided by tokens. In the lecture, 20 merges turned about 24,000 bytes into about 19,000 tokens, a ratio of about 1.27.
deep:
```python
def get_stats(ids):
    c = {}
    for p in zip(ids, ids[1:]): c[p] = c.get(p, 0) + 1
    return c

def merge(ids, pair, new):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i < len(ids) - 1 and (ids[i], ids[i + 1]) == pair: out.append(new); i += 2
        else: out.append(ids[i]); i += 1
    return out

def train(text, vocab_size):
    ids, merges = list(text.encode('utf-8')), {}
    for i in range(vocab_size - 256):               # 276 means exactly 20 merges
        stats = get_stats(ids)
        pair = max(stats, key=stats.get)
        ids = merge(ids, pair, 256 + i)
        merges[pair] = 256 + i                      # (child1, child2) -> new token id
    return merges, ids

text = "low lower lowest newer newest wider " * 20
merges, ids = train(text, 276)
print(len(merges), len(text.encode()), len(ids))    # 20 720 80
```

`merges` is a dictionary from a pair of ids to the minted id, built in insertion order (the iteration order matters later and is guaranteed in Python 3.7 and later). The structure is a forest, not a tree: the leaves are the 256 bytes, and each merge joins two nodes. Merged tokens can be merged again (in the lecture the 20th merge combined 256 and 259 into 275). The vocabulary size is a hyperparameter: more merges give a larger vocabulary and shorter sequences. GPT-4 uses roughly 100,000.
say: To train, I choose a final vocabulary size, which is a hyperparameter, and then loop: count the pairs, take the most frequent one, mint the next id starting at two fifty six, replace it everywhere, and record the merge as a mapping from the two child ids to the new id. A vocabulary of two seventy six means exactly twenty merges. The structure is a forest, not a tree, because the leaves are the raw bytes and merged tokens can merge again. In the lecture, twenty merges compressed about twenty four thousand bytes to about nineteen thousand tokens, a ratio of about one point two seven.
must_mention: record child pair to new id
forest of merges, new tokens can merge again

followups.q: What does a larger vocabulary do?
followups.a: More merges give shorter sequences and a higher compression ratio, but a bigger embedding table and output layer.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: Why is the tokenizer a separate stage from the language model, and how does its training data matter?
plain: The tokenizer is its own component, with its own training set, trained once before the language model. The language model never takes part in that training. Afterwards the tokenizer translates between raw text and token sequences, in both directions. Usually all training text is tokenised once, stored as tokens, and the raw text is discarded. The tokenizer's data mix decides how many tokens each language gets. For example, a lot of Japanese text in its training set creates many Japanese merges, so Japanese sequences get shorter. A typical vocabulary has about 100,000 tokens.
deep:
Pipeline: (1) tokenizer training set, run byte pair encoding once to learn the merges and vocabulary (a preprocessing stage); (2) encode and decode between raw text (a sequence of Unicode code points) and token sequences; (3) tokenize the whole language model training set into a massive token sequence stored on disk, then train the language model on those tokens.

The two training sets can differ. For the tokenizer we care about many languages and about code, and the mixture determines how many merges are devoted to each, hence the token density of each kind of data. More Japanese in the tokenizer's training data means more Japanese tokens are merged and Japanese gets shorter sequences, which helps a model with a finite context.

This separation also underlies the glitch token problem: tokens learned in the tokenizer's data may never occur in the language model's data.
say: The tokenizer is a completely separate object from the language model. It has its own training set, I train it once with byte pair encoding as a preprocessing stage, and afterwards it's a translation layer between raw text and token sequences in both directions. Typically I tokenise the whole language model training set once, store the tokens, and throw away the raw text. The tokenizer's training mix matters, because the amount of each language or code in it determines how many merges that data gets, and so how dense its tokens are. More Japanese there means shorter Japanese sequences.
must_mention: language model trained on stored tokens

followups.q: Can the two training sets differ?
followups.a: Yes, and they often do. That mismatch is behind glitch tokens.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How does decoding work, and why can it raise an error unless you use errors replace?
plain: To decode, look up the bytes of each token, join them, and decode the bytes as UTF-8 (a way to turn text into bytes). First build a table from token id to bytes. The first 256 ids are single bytes. Each merged id is the bytes of its first child joined with its second, in merge order. The error comes from the last step, because not every byte sequence is valid UTF-8. For example, token 128 alone is not a valid start byte, so strict decoding fails. Using errors replace puts a replacement character in its place.
deep:
```python
merges = {(101, 32): 256}                          # a tiny example table
vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)}
for (a, b), idx in merges.items():                 # insertion order matters
    vocab[idx] = vocab[a] + vocab[b]               # bytes concatenation

def decode(ids):
    return b"".join(vocab[i] for i in ids).decode('utf-8', errors='replace')

print(decode([104, 256, 105]), repr(decode([128])), decode([97]))
# he i '�' a      (token 256 is the bytes 'e ')
```

UTF-8 has a strict format: a byte of the form binary `10xxxxxx` can only continue a multi byte character, so a lone 128 (binary 10000000) is an invalid start byte, and `bytes.decode` raises an error in the default strict mode. Other modes for `errors` exist, and replace substitutes the character U+FFFD. This is what OpenAI's released code does too.

If you ever see that replacement character in a model's output, the model emitted a token sequence that is not valid UTF-8. Dictionary iteration order matters when building `vocab`, and is guaranteed to be insertion order from Python 3.7.
say: Decoding looks up the bytes for each token id, joins them all, and decodes the result as UTF-8. I build a vocab dictionary: the first two fifty six ids map to single bytes, and each merged id maps to the bytes of its first child plus the bytes of its second, in merge order. The catch is that not every byte sequence is valid UTF-8. A lone token one twenty eight starts with a continuation pattern, so strict decoding raises an error. So I decode with errors set to replace, which inserts a replacement character. If I see that character in model output, the model produced an invalid sequence.
must_mention: id to bytes table built in merge order
not all byte sequences are valid UTF-8
token 128 is an invalid start byte

followups.q: What does seeing the replacement character in output mean?
followups.a: The model predicted a token sequence that is not valid UTF-8.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How does encoding work, and in what order must merges be applied?
plain: To encode, turn the text into UTF-8 bytes (a way to turn text into bytes), then apply the learned merges in the order they were learned. Early merges must go first, because later merges are built from earlier ones. In a loop, count the pairs in the current sequence. Among those found in the merge table, take the one with the lowest merge index, and merge it. Stop when no pair is in the table. Return strings of fewer than 2 tokens unchanged. For example, with merges 256 then 257, the pair for 256 is always applied first.
deep:
```python
def get_stats(ids):
    c = {}
    for p in zip(ids, ids[1:]): c[p] = c.get(p, 0) + 1
    return c

def merge(ids, pair, new):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i < len(ids) - 1 and (ids[i], ids[i + 1]) == pair: out.append(new); i += 2
        else: out.append(ids[i]); i += 1
    return out

def encode(text, merges):
    ids = list(text.encode('utf-8'))
    while len(ids) >= 2:                                        # nothing to merge otherwise
        stats = get_stats(ids)
        pair = min(stats, key=lambda p: merges.get(p, float('inf')))   # earliest learned merge
        if pair not in merges:
            break                                               # no mergeable pair left
        ids = merge(ids, pair, merges[pair])
    return ids

merges = {(101, 32): 256, (256, 116): 257}                      # e+space, then (e space)+t
print(encode("be tea", merges))                               # [98, 257, 101, 97]
```

The `float('inf')` fallback marks pairs that are not in the merge table, so they never win the `min`. If nothing is mergeable, `min` returns an arbitrary first pair that is not in `merges`, which is the signal to break. With fewer than 2 tokens, `stats` is empty and `min` fails, hence the `len(ids) >= 2` guard.

Correctness checks: `decode(encode(s)) == s` should hold for any string, but `encode(decode(ids)) == ids` need not hold, because not every token sequence is valid UTF-8, so the identity goes one way only. The lecture verifies it on the training text and on unseen validation text.
say: To encode, I convert the text to UTF-8 bytes and then apply the learned merges in the order they were learned, since later merges depend on earlier ones. In a loop, I count the pairs in the current sequence, and among the pairs that appear in the merge table I take the one with the lowest merge index, using infinity for pairs that aren't in the table. If the best pair isn't in the table, nothing is mergeable and I stop. I also guard against sequences shorter than two tokens. Decode of encode gives back the string, but the reverse isn't guaranteed.
must_mention: pick the pair with the lowest merge index
infinity for pairs not in the table

followups.q: Is encode the inverse of decode?
followups.a: Only one way: decode of encode returns the text, but arbitrary token sequences may not be valid UTF-8.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: Why does the GPT-2 tokenizer split text with a regular expression before byte pair encoding?
plain: The tokenizer of generative pretrained transformer 2 (GPT-2) first cuts text into chunks and only merges inside each chunk, so some merges can never happen. Without this, a common word like dog would merge with nearby punctuation. For example, dog could merge with a full stop, an exclamation mark or a question mark. That mixes meaning with punctuation, which wastes tokens. A regular expression (a pattern for matching text) splits text into letters, numbers, punctuation and spaces. Each chunk is tokenised on its own, and the results are joined. So hello world 123 splits into hello, space world, and 123.
deep:
GPT-2 paper: applying plain byte pair encoding would merge dog with all punctuation (dog., dog!, dog?), producing many near duplicate tokens and mixing semantics with punctuation, which experiments showed is suboptimal. So rules are enforced top down: some character types are never merged.

The pattern (in the GPT-2 code, using the `regex` package, an extension of `re` that supports `\p{L}`) is an OR of alternatives, tried left to right: common contractions (`'s`, `'t`, `'re`, ...), an optional space followed by one or more letters, an optional space followed by numbers, an optional space followed by punctuation (not letter, number or space), and whitespace (with a negative lookahead so that the last space stays attached to the next word).

A simplified version with the standard `re` module:

```python
import re
pat = re.compile(r"'s|'t|'re|'ve|'m|'ll|'d| ?[^\W\d_]+| ?\d+| ?[^\s\w]+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+")
print(pat.findall("Hello world123 how are you? don't"))
# ['Hello', ' world', '123', ' how', ' are', ' you', '?', ' don', "'t"]
```

Each chunk is tokenised independently and the token lists are concatenated, so merges never cross chunk boundaries (for example the e and the following space are never merged). Quirks: the apostrophe rules are hard coded (the Unicode apostrophe is not matched) and are case sensitive (the GPT-2 docs say ignore case should have been used). The training code of the GPT-2 tokenizer was never released, only inference, and spaces are never merged, a rule the code does not show.
say: GPT-2 first splits the text into chunks using a regular expression, and runs byte pair encoding inside each chunk only, so merges never cross chunk boundaries. The reason is that plain byte pair encoding would merge a common word like dog with every punctuation mark next to it, mixing meaning with punctuation. The pattern separates contractions, runs of letters with an optional leading space, runs of numbers, runs of punctuation, and whitespace. So letters, digits and punctuation never merge together. It has quirks, like hard coded lowercase apostrophes, and OpenAI never released the training code.
must_mention: regex chunks by letters, numbers, punctuation, spaces
optional leading space stays with the word

followups.q: What are the pattern's quirks?
followups.a: Apostrophe rules are hard coded and case sensitive, so uppercase contractions and Unicode apostrophes split differently.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: What is tiktoken, and what changed between the GPT-2 and GPT-4 patterns?
plain: tiktoken is OpenAI's tokenizer library, and it only runs a trained tokenizer. It cannot train one. The pattern of generative pretrained transformer 4 (GPT-4), called cl100k_base, changed in three ways. First, it ignores case, so apostrophe s and apostrophe S are split the same way. Second, numbers merge at most 3 digits at a time, which avoids very long number tokens. Third, whitespace is handled differently, so runs of spaces can merge. The vocabulary grew from about 50,000 to about 100,000.
deep:
`tiktoken` (a Rust backed Python library) is inference only: it can tokenize with GPT-2 or GPT-4 (`cl100k_base`) vocabularies, but it does not provide training.

Changes in the GPT-4 chunking pattern, as shown in the lecture (the lecture does not claim to know why, because none of it is documented):

- The case insensitive flag, so the apostrophe contractions are matched in lowercase and uppercase (fixing the GPT-2 inconsistency).
- Numbers match only 1 to 3 digits, so merges never create tokens for long digit sequences.
- Different whitespace handling: in GPT-2 each space stays a separate token, whereas in GPT-4 runs of spaces merge.
- Other special tokens (end of text, plus fill in the middle tokens).

The GPT-2 pattern in `tiktoken` is equivalent to the original but runs a little faster. Both are public, since inference requires it.
say: tiktoken is OpenAI's tokenizer library, but it's inference only, so it can encode and decode with GPT-2 or GPT-4 vocabularies but can't train one. The GPT-4 splitting pattern changed in a few ways. It's case insensitive, so apostrophe contractions are handled the same in upper and lower case. Numbers merge at most three digits at a time, which prevents tokens for long digit strings. And whitespace is handled differently, so runs of spaces can merge, which is better for code. The vocabulary also grew from about fifty thousand to about a hundred thousand tokens, though none of the reasons are documented.

followups.q: Why limit numbers to 3 digits?
followups.a: It prevents very long number tokens. The lecture notes that the reasons are not documented.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: What are special tokens, and where does the number 50,257 come from?
plain: Special tokens are extra tokens that mark structure, and they are added outside the byte pair encoding. The vocabulary of generative pretrained transformer 2 (GPT-2) has 50,257 tokens. That is 256 raw byte tokens, plus 50,000 merges, plus 1 special token. The special token is end of text, which separates documents in the training stream. The model must learn that it means the earlier text is unrelated to what follows. Chat models also add tokens that mark the start and end of each message. If user text can contain such a string, it may be parsed as the special token, which is risky.
deep:
GPT-2: $256+50{,}000+1=50{,}257$. The last token, `<|endoftext|>` (id 50256), delimits documents in the training data. The data is a stream of tokens in 0 to 50255 with the special token inserted between documents.

```python
print(256 + 50000 + 1)   # 50257
```

Special tokens do not go through the merges. The tokenizer code has special case handling (in tiktoken's Rust code) to swap them in when it sees the string, and extra special tokens can be registered with new ids.

GPT-4 (`cl100k_base`): end of text, plus 4 more: fill in the middle (FIM) prefix, middle and suffix, and another special token. Chat models such as GPT-3.5 Turbo add tokens such as start and end of message to delimit conversations between user and assistant.

Security note from the lecture: the string end of text in a user prompt could be parsed as the real special token if the API allows it, making special tokens an attack surface. Asking GPT-4 to print the string end of text led to odd refusals.
say: Special tokens are extra tokens that mark structure, and they sit outside the normal merge process. GPT-2's vocabulary of fifty thousand two hundred fifty seven is the two hundred fifty six raw bytes, plus fifty thousand merges, plus one special token, end of text, which separates documents in the training stream. The model has to learn that it means the earlier document is irrelevant. GPT-4 adds tokens for fill in the middle, and chat models add message start and end tokens. One caution is that if user text is allowed to parse as a special token, that becomes an attack surface.
must_mention: 256 bytes plus 50,000 merges plus 1 special token
special token strings are an attack surface

followups.q: Why can special tokens be a security risk?
followups.a: If user text containing the special token string is parsed as the real token, it can disrupt the model.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How do you add new tokens to a pretrained model?
plain: Adding a token means resizing two parts of the network. The embedding table needs one more row for the new token. Start that row with small random numbers. The final linear layer, which makes a score for each token, needs one more output. For example, going from 50,257 to 50,258 tokens turns the embedding table into 50,258 rows. A common approach is to freeze the base model and train only the new parameters. This is how chat tokens are added when a base model becomes a chat model.
deep:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
E = rng.standard_normal((50257, 8))               # embedding table, one row per token
W = rng.standard_normal((8, 50257))               # final linear layer, one column per token
E = np.vstack([E, 0.02 * rng.standard_normal((1, 8))])    # new row, small random numbers
W = np.hstack([W, 0.02 * rng.standard_normal((8, 1))])    # new output column
print(E.shape, W.shape)                           # (50258, 8) (8, 50258)
```

Both pieces are mild model surgery: extend the embedding matrix by a row (random init) and extend the output projection by one, so the model can compute the probability of the new token. It is very common when fine tuning, for example turning a base model into a chat model with message delimiter tokens, or adding tokens for tool use such as a browser. Typically you freeze the base model and train only the new parameters, and you can freeze or train arbitrary parts as you like.
say: Adding a token means resizing two things. The embedding table gets one more row, which I initialise with small random numbers. And the final linear layer that produces the logits gets one more output, so the model can compute a probability for the new token. That's mild model surgery. It's very common when fine tuning, for example to add chat message delimiters or tokens for using tools. A typical approach is to freeze the base model and train only the new parameters. I can freeze or train any parts I like.
must_mention: add a row to the embedding table
add an output to the final linear layer
common when turning base into chat models

followups.q: Why must the output layer also change?
followups.a: The model needs a score for every token it can produce, so a new token needs a new output.

topic: Zero to Hero V9: GPT tokenizer
q: How does SentencePiece differ from tiktoken?
plain: SentencePiece can both train and run a tokenizer, and it works on code points, not bytes. tiktoken only runs a trained tokenizer, and it merges UTF-8 bytes (a way to turn text into bytes). Llama and Mistral use SentencePiece. It runs byte pair encoding directly on Unicode code points. Rare code points either become an unknown token or, with byte fallback on, are split into their UTF-8 bytes. It also has many options, such as normalisation, sentences and a dummy prefix space.
