plain: Transfer learning means reusing what a model learned on one task as the starting point for another. Ten years ago, a team would train a separate model for each task, such as spam detection or sentiment. But those tasks all need an understanding of language, so much of the learning can be shared. LLMs follow this idea in two stages: pretraining, then tuning. Pretraining teaches the model language and code from huge amounts of data. Tuning then adapts the pretrained weights to a specific task or behavior. For example, 1 pretrained model can be tuned into a spam detector and a sentiment classifier.
deep:
Traditional approach: for each task you train a dedicated model, with a training set, a validation set and a test set (spam detection, sentiment extraction, and so on). But the tasks are not disjoint, since they all involve understanding text. Transfer learning avoids starting from scratch: begin from a pretrained model and tune it for your task.

LLM recipe:

1. Pretraining: train the model on vast amounts of data to understand language and code. This is the most expensive stage.
2. Tuning: take the pretrained model and adjust its weights to a specific task or behavior (supervised fine tuning, then preference tuning, which together are called alignment).

The point is that new models are not trained from scratch for each use. The same base can be tuned for spam detection, sentiment extraction or acting as a chat assistant.
say: Transfer learning means starting from a model that already learned something useful instead of training from scratch. Ten years ago you'd train a separate model for spam detection, another for sentiment, and so on, even though they all need an understanding of language. LLMs follow this idea in two stages. Pretraining teaches the model language and code from huge amounts of data by predicting the next token, and tuning then adapts the pretrained weights to a task or behavior. So one pretrained model can become a spam detector, a sentiment classifier or a chat assistant, without starting over.
must_mention: reuse a pretrained model as the starting point
tuning adapts weights to a task
no training from scratch per task

followups.q: What is the first stage of LLM training?
followups.a: Pretraining on vast data to predict the next token, which gives general language and code understanding.

followups.q: What does the second stage do?
followups.a: Adapts the pretrained weights to a task or behavior, for example with supervised fine tuning.

traps: Saying every new use needs a model trained from scratch.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is LLM pretraining, what data does it use, and how big is it?
plain: Pretraining trains a model to predict the next token over a huge collection of text and code. It is by far the most expensive stage of training, in compute and money. Data sources include Common Crawl (a public archive of web pages), Wikipedia, Reddit, GitHub and Stack Overflow. Common Crawl adds about 3 billion pages every month. Size is counted in tokens, from hundreds of billions to tens of trillions. For example, GPT-3 (generative pretrained transformer 3) saw about 300 billion tokens, and Llama 3 about 15 trillion. The model learns the structure of languages and code, with no labels needed.
deep:
Objective: next token prediction over a decoder only model (more than 90 percent of LLMs). The model takes input text and iteratively predicts the next token.

Data: essentially everything you can find: text in English and other languages, code in many languages, the whole internet. Named sources:

- Common Crawl: an archive of web pages (about 3 billion pages per month).
- Wikipedia articles and social media such as Reddit conversations.
- Code from GitHub and Stack Overflow and other code forums.

Size is measured in tokens. Order of magnitude: hundreds of billions to tens of trillions. GPT-3 was trained on 300 billion tokens, and Llama 3 (published the year before the lecture) on 15 trillion.

Cost: pretraining is the most expensive part of training in compute and money. Its purpose is to teach the model the structure of language and code, which later tuning builds on.
say: Pretraining trains a decoder only model to predict the next token over an enormous corpus: web pages from Common Crawl, Wikipedia, Reddit conversations, and code from GitHub and Stack Overflow. Common Crawl alone adds about three billion pages a month. Data size is measured in tokens, from hundreds of billions to tens of trillions. GPT-3 saw about 300 billion tokens and Llama 3 about 15 trillion. No labels are needed, so the model just learns the structure of language and code. It's by far the most expensive stage, in compute and in money.
must_mention: web, Wikipedia, Reddit and code data

followups.q: Why does pretraining need no labels?
followups.a: The next token in the text is the label, so the data labels itself.

followups.q: How is dataset size measured?
followups.a: In tokens, from hundreds of billions to tens of trillions.

traps: Saying pretraining data is hand labeled.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is the difference between FLOPs and FLOPS, and how much compute does training an LLM take?
plain: FLOPs (floating point operations) counts the total amount of work, like additions and multiplications. FLOPS (floating point operations per second) measures hardware speed. A floating point number is just a number with a decimal point. Training a large language model takes on the order of 10 to the power of 25 FLOPs. Training work grows with the number of parameters times the number of training tokens. A common estimate is 6 operations per parameter per token. For example, 6 times 175 billion times 300 billion is about 3.2 times 10 to the power of 23. A GPU spec sheet lists FLOPS, so a faster GPU finishes the same FLOPs sooner.
deep:
FLOPs (small s): the number of operations on floating point numbers, a unit of compute. The higher the FLOPs, the more operations. Training an LLM is on the order of $10^{25}$ FLOPs. There is no universal formula (it depends on the architecture, for example a mixture of experts model activates only part of the network), but you can think of it as roughly the product of the number of training tokens and the number of parameters.

A standard estimate is $C\approx6ND$, with $N$ parameters and $D$ tokens (the factor 6 is standard background: about 2 for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass per parameter per token). Checks: GPT-3 gives $6\cdot175\cdot10^9\cdot300\cdot10^9=3.15\times10^{23}$, and Llama 3 405B on 15 trillion tokens gives $3.6\times10^{25}$, matching the quoted $10^{25}$ scale.

FLOPS (capital S): floating point operations per second, the speed of the hardware. GPU descriptions list it per number format. On the H100 slide the lecture shows 34 teraFLOPS for FP64 and about double for FP32. Papers sometimes use one spelling for the other, so read the notation in context.
say: FLOPs with a small s counts floating point operations, the total work of a computation, while FLOPS in capital letters is operations per second, the speed of the hardware. Training an LLM is on the order of ten to the twenty fifth FLOPs, and it scales roughly with the number of parameters times the number of training tokens, with six operations per parameter per token as a common estimate. For example, six times 175 billion times 300 billion is about three times ten to the twenty third, which is GPT-3. Papers sometimes mix the two spellings, so I read them in context.
must_mention: FLOPs: total operations, FLOPS: operations per second
LLM training is about 10 to the 25 FLOPs

followups.q: How would you estimate the compute of a training run?
followups.a: About 6 times parameters times training tokens.

followups.q: Why does a mixture of experts model need fewer FLOPs?
followups.a: Only the selected experts are active for each token.

traps: Treating FLOPs and FLOPS as the same thing.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What do neural scaling laws say, and what is meant by sample efficiency?
plain: Scaling laws describe how a model's loss (its prediction error) falls as you add compute, data or parameters. A 2020 paper on scaling laws for neural language models ran many experiments to measure this. It found that more compute, more data and a bigger model all lead to better next token prediction. This pushed labs to build bigger and bigger models between about 2019 and 2024. The paper also found that bigger models are more sample efficient. That means that for the same number of tokens processed, a bigger model reaches a lower loss. For example, after seeing 10 billion tokens, a 10 billion parameter model would typically beat a 1 billion parameter model.
deep:
Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models: by varying compute, dataset size and model size, they found that next token prediction improves as each increases (as smooth power laws, standard background). So bigger training sets and bigger models each help, which explains why models between 2019 and 2024 kept getting larger.

Sample efficiency: for an equal number of processed tokens, a bigger model performs better than a smaller one.

Architecture details matter little: the lecture says the paper reports that what changes performance most is the number of training tokens and the model size. Everyone uses decoder only transformers, so "LLM" here means that.

But compute is limited and expensive, so the practical question is how to split a fixed budget between model size and data. That is what the Chinchilla analysis answers.
say: Scaling laws describe how the loss falls, following a power law, as you increase compute, data and model size. The 2020 paper on scaling laws for neural language models showed that more of each gives better next token prediction, which is why labs built bigger models between about 2019 and 2024. It also found that bigger models are more sample efficient, meaning that for the same number of tokens a bigger model reaches a lower loss. The architecture details mattered much less than parameters, tokens and compute. The open question was how to split a fixed budget, which is what Chinchilla answered.
must_mention: loss falls with compute, data and model size
bigger models are more sample efficient
fixed budget split is the open question

followups.q: What does sample efficient mean?
followups.a: A bigger model reaches a given loss after fewer tokens than a smaller one.

followups.q: What is the practical limit on scaling?
followups.a: Compute is limited and expensive, so you must choose how to split a budget between parameters and tokens.

traps: Saying a bigger model is always the best use of a fixed budget.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is the Chinchilla scaling law, and was GPT-3 trained compute optimally?
plain: For a fixed compute budget, there is a best split between model size and training data. Chinchilla found that the best training set is about 20 tokens for every parameter. So a 70 billion parameter model should see about 1.4 trillion tokens. A model trained on far fewer tokens than that is called undertrained. GPT-3 had 175 billion parameters but saw only 300 billion tokens, so it was undertrained by this rule. The rule would ask for about 3.5 trillion tokens for a model of that size, roughly 12 times more. Big labs repeat this study on small models for their own setup and extrapolate, as the Llama 3 paper did.
deep:
Experiment: fix a compute budget (one color per curve in the paper's plot), train models of different sizes with different training set sizes, and look at the loss. For every budget there is a sweet spot. The resulting table of optimal parameter and token counts is sometimes called the Chinchilla law: a training set of about 20 times the model size, in tokens, spends compute optimally:

$$
D\approx20\,N
$$

Combined with $C\approx6ND$ this gives $C\approx120N^2$, so $N=\sqrt{C/120}$ and $D=20N$. For $C=10^{24}$: $N\approx91$ billion parameters and $D\approx1.8$ trillion tokens.

GPT-3: 175 billion parameters would call for $20\times175=3{,}500$ billion tokens, but it saw 300 billion (11.7 times fewer), so by this rule it is undertrained.

Setup dependence (Q and A): the exact relation depends on the architecture and data, so labs reproduce the analysis for their own models. The Llama 3 paper has a section fitting the optimal tokens and parameters at a fixed compute on small runs and extrapolating to justify the 405 billion parameter size. (Llama 3 then trained on 15 trillion tokens, about 37 per parameter, which exceeds 20. This overtraining comes from inference cost considerations, standard background not covered in the lecture.)
say: For a fixed compute budget, Chinchilla found a sweet spot between model size and data: about twenty training tokens per parameter. So a 70 billion parameter model should see about 1.4 trillion tokens. Using that rule, GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters and only 300 billion tokens, was undertrained. It would have wanted around 3.5 trillion, about twelve times more. In practice labs rerun this kind of study on small models for their own setup and extrapolate, as the Llama 3 paper did. One caveat is that it optimizes training compute only, and inference cost can push you toward smaller models trained longer.
must_mention: fixed compute has a sweet spot
labs rerun the analysis for their setup

followups.q: How many tokens does a 70 billion parameter model want?
followups.a: About 1.4 trillion, by the 20 tokens per parameter rule.

followups.q: Why might a lab train beyond the Chinchilla optimum?
followups.a: A smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve, so inference cost can outweigh the training optimum.

traps: Saying Chinchilla says to make the model as large as possible.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What are the main challenges of pretraining an LLM?
plain: Cost is the first challenge: pretraining costs millions of dollars at minimum, and often tens or hundreds of millions. It also takes a long time and has an environmental cost. The second is the knowledge cutoff date: the model knows nothing from after its training data ends. For example, a model with a cutoff of September 30 cannot know about events in October. Editing or adding knowledge afterwards is hard, because changing weights for one fact can hurt other skills. The third is plagiarism risk: the model may reproduce text it saw in training. Model cards on provider websites list the knowledge cutoff date for this reason.
deep:
1. Cost: millions of dollars at the minimum, possibly tens or even hundreds of millions, and a lot of time. People have also become mindful of the ecological cost and now report it.
2. Knowledge cutoff date: pretraining uses data up to a date, so a pretrained base model cannot know anything that happened later. Model cards list the cutoff (the lecture's example: a GPT-5 card giving September 30, which hints at when pretraining was done).
3. Editing knowledge: many papers try to edit or inject knowledge, but there is no clean way to change the weights without penalizing other parts. The aim is to inject knowledge without regressing in other domains, which is very hard.
4. Plagiarism or memorization: the model predicts the next token, so it may generate something it saw at training time.

Standard mitigations (background, not in the lecture): retrieval for fresh facts (Lecture 7), tuning for behavior, and data filtering for memorization.
say: Pretraining has three main challenges. Cost: at least millions of dollars, often tens or hundreds of millions, plus a long time and an environmental footprint. Knowledge cutoff: the model knows nothing after the end of its data, and model cards list the cutoff date, for example September 30 for one recent model. Editing knowledge afterward is hard because changing weights for one fact can hurt other abilities. And there's plagiarism risk, since the model can reproduce text it saw. Fine tuning helps with behavior, but fresh facts usually need retrieval.

followups.q: Why can't you just patch a wrong fact in the weights?
followups.a: Weights are shared across skills, so changing them for one fact can hurt other abilities, and there is no clean method.

followups.q: How do you give a model fresh facts?
followups.a: Usually retrieval at inference time, because updating weights is costly and risky.

traps: Assuming a model knows recent events because it can chat about them.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What has to be kept in GPU memory when training an LLM, and why does one GPU not suffice?
plain: Training has four steps: a forward pass, a loss, a backward pass and a weight update. The forward pass produces activations, the values at each layer that are needed for the loss. The backward pass computes gradients (the direction that lowers the loss) for every parameter. The Adam optimizer (a popular weight update method) also keeps two running averages per parameter, called moments. Activation memory grows with model size, batch size and context length. One H100 GPU has 80 gigabytes of memory, which is not enough for large models. For example, 7 billion parameters at about 16 bytes each need 112 gigabytes, more than one 80 gigabyte GPU. So training is spread over many GPUs.
deep:
Steps and what each leaves in memory:

1. Forward pass: pass a batch through the network and keep the activations (values per layer needed to compute the loss). Activation memory depends on the model size, the batch size and the context length, since attention is $O(n^2)$ in the sequence length $n$.
2. Loss: how far you are from the label.
3. Backward pass: the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter (the direction that minimizes the loss). Gradients must be stored too.
4. Weight update with an optimizer such as Adam, which keeps the first moment (a moving average of the gradient) and the second moment (a moving average of the squared gradient) per parameter, also stored:

$$
m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2
$$

An H100 has 80 GB of GPU memory, which is quite large but not a lot given all of this. A standard accounting for mixed precision Adam (background from the ZeRO paper) is 2 bytes of FP16 weights, 2 of FP16 gradients and 12 of FP32 master weights and moments, so 16 bytes per parameter: $7\times10^9\times16=112$ GB before activations. Hence the parallelism methods that follow. (Google trains on its own TPUs, while other models mostly use GPUs.)
say: Training has a forward pass, a loss, a backward pass and a weight update, and each leaves something in memory. The forward pass keeps activations, which grow with model size, batch size and context length. The backward pass produces gradients, and Adam keeps two running averages per parameter, the first and second moments. With mixed precision that's about sixteen bytes per parameter, so a 7 billion parameter model needs around 112 gigabytes, more than one 80 gigabyte H100. That's why training spreads across many GPUs, using data parallelism, ZeRO and model parallelism.
must_mention: activation memory grows with size, batch and context
80 GB per GPU is not enough

followups.q: What are Adam's two moments?
followups.a: Moving averages of the gradient (first moment) and of the squared gradient (second moment).

followups.q: Why does context length affect memory?
followups.a: Self attention is quadratic in sequence length, so activations grow quickly with it.

traps: Counting only the weights when estimating training memory.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: How do data parallelism and ZeRO distribute training across GPUs?
plain: Data parallelism gives every GPU a full copy of the model and a different slice of each batch. Each GPU runs its own forward and backward pass, and the gradients are averaged across GPUs. This cuts the memory tied to batch size, but adds communication between GPUs. It also needs the whole model to fit on each GPU. ZeRO (zero redundancy optimizer) removes the duplicate copies by splitting them across GPUs. Stage 1 splits the optimizer states, stage 2 also splits the gradients, and stage 3 also splits the parameters. Higher stages save more memory per GPU but need more communication. For example, with 8 GPUs, a 112 gigabyte training state split fully takes about 14 gigabytes per GPU.
deep:
Data parallelism (DP): divide the batch across devices and keep a copy of the model per device, so forward and backward passes run independently. This reduces the memory tied to the batch size. The gradient is the average of the per device gradients, so the GPUs communicate to aggregate it. Cons: a communication cost (training is slower than ideal) and each device must hold the whole model.

ZeRO (zero redundancy optimizer): in plain DP each GPU stores the same parameters, gradients and optimizer states, which is redundant. ZeRO shards them:

| Stage | Sharded across GPUs | Bytes per parameter per GPU ($N_d$ GPUs, mixed precision Adam) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | optimizer states | $2+2+12/N_d$ |
| 2 | plus gradients | $2+14/N_d$ |
| 3 | plus parameters | $16/N_d$ |

(Memory column is standard background.) Cost: more communication at higher stages. The stage you choose depends on how sensitive you are to training time and how big the model is. Check: 7 billion parameters, 8 GPUs, stage 3: $7\cdot10^9\cdot16/8=14$ GB per GPU before activations.
say: In data parallelism each GPU holds a full copy of the model and processes a different slice of the batch, then the gradients are averaged across GPUs. It reduces the memory tied to batch size but adds communication, and every GPU still needs to fit the whole model. ZeRO removes that duplication by sharding: stage one splits the optimizer states, stage two also the gradients, and stage three also the parameters. Each stage saves more memory per GPU but needs more communication. For example, fully sharding 112 gigabytes over eight GPUs leaves about 14 gigabytes each, before activations.
must_mention: full model copy per GPU, split batch
communication cost and model must fit
higher stage saves memory, costs communication

followups.q: What does each ZeRO stage shard?
followups.a: Stage 1 the optimizer states, stage 2 adds the gradients, stage 3 adds the parameters.

followups.q: What is the downside of ZeRO 3?
followups.a: Parameters must be gathered when needed, so communication grows.

traps: Saying data parallelism splits the model. It splits the batch.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What are expert, tensor and pipeline parallelism?
plain: Model parallelism splits the model itself across graphics processing units (GPUs), instead of splitting the data. Expert parallelism puts different experts of a mixture of experts model on different GPUs. Tensor parallelism cuts a big matrix multiplication into pieces that run on different GPUs. Pipeline parallelism gives each GPU a group of consecutive layers, so the forward pass moves from GPU to GPU. Each method lowers the memory needed on a single GPU and adds communication. In practice, large runs combine data parallelism with these methods. For example, 32 layers on 4 GPUs gives 8 consecutive layers to each GPU.
deep:
Model parallelism parallelizes the operations within one batch, in contrast to data parallelism, which handles separate slices of data. The lecture's catalog (no need to know the details, just a rough idea):

- Expert parallelism: for mixture of experts LLMs, place one expert (or a few) per device, and route each token's computation to the device holding its expert.
- Tensor parallelism: split a large matrix multiplication into parts across devices to cut the memory required for it.
- Pipeline parallelism: a forward pass has several layers, so assign layers 1 to 3 to one GPU, 4 to 6 to another, and so on.

All lower per device memory, so a model that does not fit on one GPU can be trained, at the price of communication (and, for pipelines, idle time called bubbles, standard background). Real systems combine data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, sometimes with expert parallelism.
say: Model parallelism splits the model itself across devices. Expert parallelism puts different experts of a mixture of experts model on different GPUs. Tensor parallelism cuts a big matrix multiplication into pieces on different GPUs. Pipeline parallelism assigns consecutive layers to each GPU, so a forward pass moves from device to device, for example layers one to eight on the first of four GPUs for a 32 layer model. Each lowers per GPU memory at the price of communication, and large runs combine them with data parallelism. I'd know the rough idea of each rather than the details.
must_mention: expert parallelism: experts on different devices

followups.q: How does pipeline parallelism differ from tensor parallelism?
followups.a: Pipeline splits between layers (each GPU owns whole layers), tensor splits inside a layer's matrix multiplication.

followups.q: Why combine these methods?
followups.a: Each handles a different bottleneck, and big models need several together.

traps: Mixing up data parallelism, which splits the batch, with model parallelism, which splits the network.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: How does FlashAttention speed up attention without approximating it?
plain: FlashAttention computes exact attention faster by cutting down slow memory traffic on the GPU. A GPU has large but slower memory called high bandwidth memory (HBM). It also has tiny but much faster memory on the chip, called static random access memory (SRAM). Plain attention writes big intermediate matrices to HBM and reads them back, and that traffic is the bottleneck. FlashAttention cuts the inputs into small blocks, called tiles, and does the whole computation for a block inside SRAM. Only the final result goes back to HBM. The result is exactly the same as normal attention, only computed in a smarter order. For example, SRAM is about 10 times faster than HBM but roughly 1,000 times smaller.
deep:
GPU memory has two kinds: HBM, big (tens of gigabytes, the GPU memory on the spec sheet) but slower (a few terabytes per second), and SRAM, on chip next to the compute, tiny (tens of megabytes) but about 10 times faster (tens of terabytes per second).

Vanilla attention $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$, with matrices of $n$ rows ($n$ the sequence length): read $Q,K$ from HBM, compute $QK^\top$, write it back; read it, compute the softmax, write it back; read it and $V$, multiply, write the output. Many HBM reads and writes make data transfer the bottleneck, even though the GPU compute is very fast.

FlashAttention (Stanford, 2022; Fast and memory efficient exact attention with IO awareness) uses tiling: send small blocks of the inputs to SRAM, compute end to end there, and write back only the output, minimizing HBM traffic. The softmax makes this non obvious (each row must be normalized), which the next card resolves. It is exact: no approximation, only a cleverer schedule of the same computation. Versions 2 and 3 adapt the idea to each new GPU generation's strengths and weaknesses.
say: FlashAttention computes exact attention faster by reducing traffic to slow GPU memory. A GPU has big but slower high bandwidth memory, HBM, and a tiny but roughly ten times faster on chip memory, SRAM. Standard attention writes the big score matrix to HBM and reads it back several times, and that traffic is the bottleneck. FlashAttention tiles the computation: it loads small blocks into SRAM, finishes the softmax and the output for the block there, and writes only the result back. It makes no approximation. It came out of Stanford in 2022, with later versions adapted to new GPUs.
must_mention: HBM is big and slow, SRAM is tiny and fast
standard attention is bound by HBM traffic

followups.q: Is FlashAttention an approximation of attention?
followups.a: No. It computes exactly the same result with fewer slow memory reads and writes.

followups.q: What is the bottleneck it removes?
followups.a: Data transfer to and from HBM, not arithmetic.

traps: Confusing it with sparse attention. FlashAttention is exact.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: How does FlashAttention compute the softmax block by block, and why does recomputation save time?
plain: Softmax needs a sum over a whole row, so it seems you must finish the full row first. The trick is that the softmax of a long row can be built from softmaxes of its pieces. Each piece is rescaled by a correction factor that is updated as new pieces arrive. At the end the pieces combine to exactly the softmax of the full row. The second idea is recomputation: do not store activations in the forward pass, and recompute them during the backward pass. Recomputing does more arithmetic, but it avoids slow memory reads, so the run is still faster. For example, memory traffic in the paper's table drops from 40.3 to about 4, nearly 10 times less.
deep:
Block by block softmax (online softmax). For one query row, process the keys and values in blocks. Keep a running maximum $m$, a running sum $\ell$ and a running unnormalized output $o$. For a new block with scores $s$ and values $v$:

$$
m'=\max\big(m,\max s\big),\qquad \ell'=e^{m-m'}\ell+\sum e^{s-m'},\qquad o'=e^{m-m'}o+\sum e^{s-m'}v
$$

After the last block the output is $o/\ell$, exactly the full softmax attention. Intuition from the lecture: the softmax is an exponential divided by a quantity shared across the row, so a scaling factor fixes the pieces. The paper spells out the formula, and the lecture says you need not memorize it. Check (numpy, 8 tokens, blocks of 2): maximum absolute difference from full attention $1.7\times10^{-16}$.

Recomputation: the chain rule in the backward pass needs activations. Since attention is now fast, do not store them in the forward pass but recompute them in the backward pass. This does more FLOPs (the lecture's table shows slightly more operations), yet it reads and writes far less from HBM (40.3 down to about 4, nearly 10 times, in the figure shown) and the runtime also falls. Usually recomputation trades time for memory, so here you get both: the best of all worlds. (I could not verify the units of the 40.3 figure beyond the slide.)
say: The obstacle is that softmax needs a normalizer over the whole row. The trick is that a row's softmax can be built block by block. For each block I keep a running maximum and a running sum of exponentials, and when a new block arrives, I rescale the old partial results by the exponential of the change in the maximum, then add the new block. At the end, dividing the accumulated output by the sum gives exactly the full softmax attention. The second idea is recomputation: I don't store activations in the forward pass, I recompute them in the backward pass. That costs extra operations but saves memory traffic, so it's both smaller and faster.
must_mention: softmax assembled from slices with a rescaling factor
recompute activations in the backward pass
more FLOPs, less memory traffic, faster

followups.q: Why do you need a running maximum?
followups.a: To keep the exponentials numerically stable and to rescale earlier partial sums when a larger score appears.

followups.q: Why is recomputation unusually free here?
followups.a: Memory traffic, not arithmetic, is the bottleneck, so extra FLOPs cost less than the HBM reads they remove.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: How are floating point numbers stored, and what is quantization?
plain: A floating point number is stored as a sign, an exponent and a mantissa. The exponent sets the range of the number, and the mantissa sets how fine its detail is. FP32 means floating point with 32 bits, and FP16 uses 16 bits, so it takes half the memory. Brain float 16 (BF16) keeps the 8 exponent bits of FP32, so it has the same range with less detail. Fewer bits means less precision, because the numbers are less fine grained. Quantization converts numbers to a lower precision format to save memory, hoping accuracy barely drops. Lower precision also runs faster: on the GPU in the lecture, FP32 doubles the speed of FP64. For example, a 7 billion parameter model takes 28 gigabytes in FP32 and 14 gigabytes in FP16.
deep:
A float is a bundle of bits: a sign bit, exponent bits (range) and mantissa bits (granularity of the number). Standard layouts (sign, exponent, mantissa):

| Format | Bits | Layout |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FP64 | 64 | 1, 11, 52 |
| FP32 (single precision) | 32 | 1, 8, 23 |
| FP16 (half precision) | 16 | 1, 5, 10 |
| BF16 (brain float) | 16 | 1, 8, 7 |

(The lecture shows the table with each format's granularity and does not list the layouts, so these are standard background.) FP16 has half the memory of FP32 but is less granular, with a maximum value near 65,504, while BF16 keeps FP32's range with coarser steps.

Quantization is the process of converting the precision of a number from one setting to another. The hope is to shrink memory and speed up compute without hurting performance. The lecture's GPU sheet shows compute speed depends on the format: 34 teraFLOPS in FP64 and about twice as much in FP32, with more speed at lower precision. Arithmetic: $7\times10^9\times4$ bytes $=28$ GB in FP32 and $7\times10^9\times2=14$ GB in FP16.

Range handling methods named in the Q and A: zero point quantization and absmax quantization. NF4 comes with QLoRA.
say: A floating point number is stored as a sign, an exponent that sets the range, and a mantissa that sets the precision. FP32 uses 32 bits and FP16 uses 16, so half the memory, but with less precision. BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range with fewer mantissa bits. Quantization converts numbers to a lower precision format to save memory, hoping accuracy barely drops, and lower precision also runs faster on GPUs: in the lecture's H100 spec, FP32 had twice the speed of FP64. For a 7 billion parameter model, FP32 weights take 28 gigabytes and FP16 take 14.
must_mention: FP16 is half the memory of FP32
quantization lowers precision to save memory

followups.q: What does the exponent control versus the mantissa?
followups.a: The exponent sets the range of values, the mantissa sets how fine the steps are.

followups.q: How much memory do 7 billion weights take in FP16?
followups.a: 14 gigabytes, two bytes each.

traps: Assuming fewer bits always keeps accuracy. It is a trade off that must be checked.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is mixed precision training, and why keep the weights in high precision?
plain: Mixed precision training uses low precision for most computation and high precision where it matters. The weights are kept in FP32 (floating point with 32 bits). The forward and backward passes run in FP16 (16 bits), which uses less memory and runs faster. The weight update is still done in FP32. The authors found that quality barely dropped, while memory use fell and speed rose. Intuition: the forward pass runs on noisy data, so extra decimals add little to the gradient direction. Weights, however, get many small updates, so low precision could pile up rounding errors. For example, an update of 0.00001 to a weight of 1.0 can vanish in FP16 but survives in FP32.
deep:
Recipe: keep the weights (master copy) in FP32. Run the forward and backward passes in FP16. Apply the weight update in FP32. In the paper the performance was not degraded much while memory dropped and training ran faster.

Why high precision for the weights (lecture's intuition): forward and backward passes run on a set of data that can be noisy, so the decimals far after the point may not matter. The gradient only says in which direction the weights should move, and does not need to be super precise. The weights themselves should stay precise to avoid accumulating errors due to quantization.

Numeric illustration: FP16 has a relative spacing near 1.0 of about $2^{-10}\approx0.001$, so $1.0+10^{-5}$ rounds back to 1.0 in FP16, while FP32 (spacing about $10^{-7}$) keeps it as $1.00001$ (checked with numpy).

Not uniform: applying it to all weights of all layers is not necessarily done, and many papers describe variations from setup to setup, since some parts matter more than others. (Loss scaling to avoid FP16 gradient underflow is standard background, not in the lecture.)
say: In mixed precision training I keep the master weights in FP32, run the forward and backward passes in FP16, and do the weight update in FP32. That saves memory and runs faster, and the authors found the quality barely dropped. The intuition is that activations and gradients come from noisy data, so extra decimals add little to the direction of the update, but the weights receive many small updates, and low precision would let rounding errors accumulate or swallow them. For example, adding 0.00001 to a weight of 1.0 vanishes in FP16 but survives in FP32. It's not applied uniformly to every layer, and setups vary.
must_mention: less memory and faster, quality barely drops
small updates would be lost in low precision

followups.q: Why can't the weight update be done in FP16?
followups.a: Small updates can be smaller than FP16's spacing and vanish, and errors accumulate over many steps.

followups.q: Is every layer treated the same?
followups.a: Not necessarily. Setups vary, since some parts are more sensitive than others.

traps: Thinking the whole network is simply cast to FP16.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: Why does a pretrained model need supervised fine tuning, and what is the SFT loss?
plain: A pretrained model only continues text, and it was never taught to be a helpful assistant. Supervised fine tuning (SFT) fixes this by training on pairs of an input and the ideal output. Supervised means the pairs carry labels, and fine tuning means further training of weights that already exist. The input is fixed, so the model is not trained to repeat it. Loss is counted only on the output tokens, which the model must predict starting from the input. For example, with a 20 token question and a 100 token answer, the loss covers only the 100 answer tokens. The model reuses what it learned in pretraining, so far less data is needed than in pretraining.
deep:
Motivation (the lecture's example): ask a pretrained model whether the teddy bear can go in the washer. It was trained on next token prediction, not on being helpful, so it will mimic likely patterns, for example another question or a sentence about what teddy bears are made of.

SFT: supervised means labeled pairs of an input and an output, and fine tuning means refining weights that were already trained. Start from the pretrained weights and train on additional data. The objective changes slightly from pretraining. Pretraining starts at BOS and predicts the next token across the whole corpus. In SFT the input (washing the teddy bear) is fixed and given, and the loss starts at the first output token:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{SFT}=-\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log p_\theta\big(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}\big)
$$

There is no loss over the input tokens and no teacher forcing on them (confirmed in the lecture Q and A). SFT can tune a model for your own task, or, as instruction tuning, turn a language model into a general assistant.
say: A pretrained model only continues text. Ask whether a teddy bear can go in the washer and it may just produce another likely sentence. Supervised fine tuning trains it on input and output pairs, starting from the pretrained weights. The loss is the usual cross entropy, but computed only on the output tokens. The input is fixed, so I don't train the model to repeat it, and there's no teacher forcing on it. After SFT, it answers the question and may suggest hand washing. It needs much less data than pretraining because it reuses what the model already knows.

followups.q: Why not put a loss on the input tokens?
followups.a: The input is given and fixed. We want the model to respond to it, not to parrot it.

followups.q: What does supervised mean here?
followups.a: The training pairs carry labels, the desired outputs.

traps: Applying the loss to the whole sequence, which trains the model to repeat prompts.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is instruction tuning, and what kinds of data go into it?
plain: Instruction tuning is supervised fine tuning that teaches a model to follow instructions. The training data is pairs of an instruction and a good response. Categories include story writing, poems, lists, explanations, math, code and assistant dialogues. Safety data teaches the model to refuse harmful requests and to hedge instead of making blanket claims. Refusals are learned by the model itself, because rules written by hand do not scale. Early data was written by humans, such as linguists writing ideal answers. Today a strong model can draft responses, and humans or another model review them. For example, Llama 3 used about 10 million such examples.
deep:
Instruction tuning is the subcategory of SFT behind the transition from a good representation of language to a useful assistant: the model should answer instructions.

Data mixture, in contrast to the raw internet of pretraining: examples that show how to respond most helpfully, in categories such as story writing, poem creation, list generation, explanation, math (writing a proof), code (high quality code bases) and assistant dialogues that mirror what users ask at inference time. Training uses the instruction as given input and fits the loss on the response.

Safety is part of the mixture: the model should be helpful but also harmless. Subsets enforce not repeating harmful content from pretraining, reject harmful prompts (done by training, only rarely via regex because regex does not scale), and use hedging to nuance outputs instead of blanket statements.

Sources: originally human written, with expert linguists writing fluent, helpful answers. Today a performant model can sample responses to instructions and a human or another LLM reviews quality, which speeds up curation.
say: Instruction tuning is the form of SFT that teaches the model to follow instructions, so it moves from a good language model to a useful assistant. The data is instruction and response pairs across categories like story writing, poems, lists, explanations, math, code and assistant dialogues, plus safety data that teaches it to refuse harmful requests and to hedge rather than make blanket claims. Refusals are learned into the model, since regex rules don't scale. Early data was written by humans, but today a strong model drafts responses and humans or another model review them. Llama 3 used about ten million examples.

followups.q: Why are refusals trained in rather than done with regex?
followups.a: Rules do not scale to the variety of harmful requests, so the behavior is embedded in the model.

followups.q: How is the data produced today?
followups.a: A strong model drafts responses, then humans or another LLM review the quality.

traps: Saying instruction data is all human written today.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: How big is SFT data compared with pretraining data, and what makes SFT hard?
plain: SFT data is counted in examples, and it is far smaller than pretraining data. GPT-3 used about 13 thousand examples, and Llama 3 used about 10 million. At roughly 1,000 tokens per example, 10 million examples is about 10 billion tokens, against 15 trillion for pretraining. That is under 0.1 percent of the pretraining size. SFT needs high quality data, which usually means people checking it, so it is costly. The prompts in training should look like the prompts users send, or the model may generalize badly. For example, a model tuned on textbook style stories may struggle with stories about movie plots. The data is reused, so the cost is paid once and can be extended over time.
deep:
Orders of magnitude (the GPT-3 and Llama 3 papers report SFT size in examples, not tokens): about 13 thousand examples for GPT-3 and 10 million for Llama 3. Assuming about 1,000 tokens per example, that is $1.3\times10^7$ tokens (0.004 percent of 300 billion) and $10^{10}$ tokens (0.067 percent of 15 trillion). So pretraining is a lot of data for general characteristics of language, while SFT aligns the model's goal to the tasks you want, with very high quality, concise data.

Challenges named in the lecture:

1. Data quality: high quality usually means humans in the loop, to make sure the data respects all the rules and characteristics users care about. It is highly involved, mixing human and generated data today. The data is reused, so it is work done once and extended over time, but still very expensive in time and resources.
2. Prompt distribution: SFT prompts should align with the inference distribution. Poetry stories generalize, but stories about movie plots may be out of distribution compared with textbook stories.
3. Generalization depends on the data mixture: points sparse enough in distribution space give the gist of what to learn, rather than repeating the same story. A model will not reproduce a training story word for word, because sampling at non zero temperature varies it, though it may keep the flavor.

Generalization beyond examples relies on knowledge from pretraining (the model already knows many kinds of poetry).
say: SFT data is counted in examples and is orders of magnitude smaller than pretraining: about 13 thousand for GPT-3 and about 10 million for Llama 3. At roughly a thousand tokens each, that's 10 billion tokens against 15 trillion, under 0.1 percent. Pretraining teaches general language, SFT aligns behavior, so quality beats quantity. It's hard because it needs high quality data, usually with humans in the loop, which is expensive, though the dataset is reusable. And the training prompts should match the prompts users send, otherwise generalization suffers, for instance from textbook stories to movie plots. Data mixture and coverage drive generalization.
must_mention: 13 thousand examples for GPT-3, 10 million for Llama 3
far below 0.1 percent of pretraining tokens
relies on pretraining knowledge to generalize

followups.q: Why does SFT work with so little data?
followups.a: The model already learned language in pretraining, so SFT only has to align its behavior.

followups.q: What goes wrong if the SFT prompts differ from user prompts?
followups.a: The model may fail to generalize to out of distribution requests.

traps: Assuming more SFT data is always better regardless of quality.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What are common LLM benchmarks, and what does training on the test task mean?
plain: Benchmarks give a number for each skill, so models can be compared. MMLU (massive multitask language understanding) tests general knowledge across many subjects. GSM8K tests grade school math, and other benchmarks test reasoning and code writing. New benchmarks keep appearing, because people tune their models for the old ones. Sometimes a model's score jumps with no clear reason. One cause is training on the test task: the model was trained on data close to the benchmark's task. To compare two models fairly, both should have had the same kind of task specific training. For example, a 10 point lead on a math benchmark may just mean more math practice in training.
deep:
Dimensions people evaluate, each with benchmarks that give a quantitative number:

- General language: MMLU (massive multitask language understanding), a single score people report, covering many tasks.
- Reasoning and math reasoning: for example GSM8K, grade school math problems (the 8K is the number of examples).
- Code generation.

Benchmark design is an active research area: more and more benchmarks appear because people optimize for existing ones, and gaps get filled by new ones.

Pattern seen as models are released: for the same kind of model, a sudden spike on some benchmark with no clear explanation. The paper recommended in the lecture studies training on the test task, not the test set: whether the model was trained on data related to the benchmark's kind of reasoning matters a lot. Benchmarks even come with auxiliary training sets for the same domain. To compare models you need parity in the training mixtures, meaning both or neither trained on the test task, otherwise the comparison does not show intrinsic value.

Another limit: since people build training data that resembles what benchmarks measure, a model can score great everywhere and still add little for you. Lecture 8 covers evaluation in depth.
say: Benchmarks put a number on a skill: MMLU for broad knowledge across many subjects, GSM8K for grade school math, and others for reasoning and code. New ones keep appearing because teams optimize for existing ones. A model's score can jump for no clear reason, and one explanation is training on the test task: the model was trained on data close to the benchmark's task, not on the test set itself. So to compare two models fairly, I'd check that both had comparable task specific training. Even then, high scores don't always translate into value for a user, so I combine several signals.
must_mention: MMLU, GSM8K, reasoning and code benchmarks
training on the test task, not the test set

followups.q: What is the difference between training on the test set and on the test task?
followups.a: The test set is the exact evaluation data. The test task is related training data from the same kind of task, which still inflates the score.

followups.q: Why do new benchmarks keep appearing?
followups.a: Teams optimize for existing ones, so gaps open and saturate.

traps: Assuming a higher benchmark score always means a more capable model for your use case.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: How does Chatbot Arena rank models, and what are its weaknesses?
plain: Chatbot Arena is a website where a user asks one question and sees answers from two models whose names are hidden. The user picks the better answer, and pairwise comparisons are turned into a ranking. This ranking measures user preference, a number put on the vibes. It is noisy for new models, because their first few opponents strongly sway the ranking. A paper showed the ranking can be rigged, since asking who are you reveals which model is which. Users cannot always judge facts, so a confident but wrong answer can win. Style matters too, such as emojis, and users tend to prefer answers over safety refusals. For example, if 100 users pick between two answers and 60 choose A, A wins 60 percent of the time.
deep:
Setup: models are submitted, users ask questions, see responses from two models and judge which is better. Pairwise computations on the site turn the votes into a ranking by user preference (a rating scheme in the Elo or Bradley Terry family, standard background).

Issues named in the lecture:

1. Noise at the start: a new model's first few comparisons influence its ranking a lot, which makes it brittle.
2. Rigging: a paper showed it is easy to rig, since models answer who are you with their name, so an adversary can detect the model under test and vote for it. The lecturer notes there is no evidence of this being done.
3. Factuality: users cannot always tell factual from non factual answers. Curated benchmarks have expert guidelines, while a user may find confident but wrong washing advice actionable.
4. Preference mismatch: for example emojis are popular in the wider population but experts may dislike them, and the people who vote differ from the wider user base.
5. Safety bias: users dislike refusals, so there is a bias toward responses that answer rather than respect a safety principle, which may be an intended product decision.

Conclusion: evaluation is hard, no single number tells you what you care about, and the combination should be tailored to your use case.
say: Chatbot Arena is a website where a user asks a question, sees answers from two models with hidden names, and picks the better one. Pairwise votes become a ranking of user preference. Its weaknesses: a new model's first few comparisons add noise that strongly sways its rank. A paper showed it can be rigged, because asking who are you reveals which model is which. Users often can't verify facts, so a fluent wrong answer can win. Style preferences like emojis and a dislike of safety refusals bias the votes. So it's one useful signal, not the truth about quality.
must_mention: noisy for new models, can be rigged

followups.q: How can the ranking be rigged?
followups.a: Asking who are you makes models reveal their identity, so an adversary can detect and vote for a chosen model.

followups.q: Why does it favor compliance over safety?
followups.a: Users dislike refusals, so answers that comply win even when the product decision is to refuse.

traps: Treating the arena rank as a measure of factual accuracy.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What do alignment and mid training mean in the LLM training pipeline?
plain: Alignment means making a model behave the way people want, helpful and harmless. It combines two steps that come after pretraining: supervised fine tuning (SFT), then preference tuning. Preference tuning, covered next lecture, adjusts the model using judgments of which answer is better. Mid training is a newer step between pretraining and fine tuning. It keeps the pretraining objective but changes the data toward the tasks you care about. The usual order is pretraining, optional mid training, SFT, then preference tuning. For example, 4 stages in order are pretraining, mid training, SFT and preference tuning.
deep:
Alignment: the combination of fine tuning (SFT) and preference tuning, both coming after pretraining. Preference tuning (RLHF, DPO and related methods) is the subject of Lecture 5.

Mid training: an emerging step between pretraining and fine tuning. It uses the same pretraining objective (next token prediction) but aligns the kind of data sets and tasks to what you care about. Typical focus areas (standard background, not named in the lecture) are code, math or long documents.

Pipeline: pretraining, then optional mid training, then SFT or instruction tuning, then preference tuning. The first stage teaches language and code, SFT teaches to follow instructions, and preference tuning refines which answers people prefer.
say: Alignment is making the model behave as people want, helpful and harmless, and it's the combination of supervised fine tuning and preference tuning after pretraining. SFT teaches it to follow instructions from labeled examples, and preference tuning, covered next, refines it using judgments of which answer is better. Mid training is a newer step between pretraining and SFT. It keeps the pretraining objective, next token prediction, but shifts the data toward the tasks and domains I care about. So the full order is pretraining, optional mid training, SFT, then preference tuning.
must_mention: alignment is SFT plus preference tuning
mid training sits between pretraining and SFT
preference tuning is the next lecture

followups.q: How does mid training differ from SFT?
followups.a: Mid training keeps the next token objective on unlabeled style data, while SFT uses labeled input and output pairs.

followups.q: What are the two steps of alignment?
followups.a: Supervised fine tuning and preference tuning.

traps: Calling pretraining the alignment step.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is LoRA, and why does it make fine tuning cheaper?
plain: Low rank adaptation (LoRA) fine tunes a model by training two small matrices instead of the big weight matrix. The original weights, called W0, stay frozen and are not changed. The update is the product of a tall matrix B and a wide matrix A. Their shared inner size is the rank r, which is tiny, often around 4 to 8. The output is the frozen layer's result plus the small update's result. Far fewer weights are trained, so less memory and compute are needed. For example, a 4,096 by 4,096 matrix has 16.8 million weights, while rank 8 matrices A and B total 65,536. Each task gets its own small A and B, so one base model can serve many tasks.
deep:
Instead of directly tuning the whole weight matrix, LoRA decomposes the weights into the pretrained part and a low rank product:

$$
W=W_0+BA,\qquad W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\ \text{(frozen)},\quad B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\quad A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k}
$$

$B$ has as many rows as $W_0$ and $A$ as many columns, and the inner dimension $r$ is the rank, typically very small (up to about 10), while $d$ and $k$ are hundreds or thousands. Trainable parameters: $r(d+k)$ instead of $dk$. For $d=k=4096$, $r=8$: $65{,}536$ against $16{,}777{,}216$, which is 256 times fewer.

Forward pass: do it on both terms and add the results, $h=W_0x+BAx$. $A$ and $B$ characterize the task, so you can start from a base model, tune $A$ and $B$ for spam detection, and keep another pair for sentiment extraction, a property that makes one base model reusable. (Standard background: $B$ is initialized to 0 so training starts exactly at the base model, and the update is scaled by $\alpha/r$.) Prefix tuning and adapters are other efficient methods, less commonly used (see the class textbook).
say: LoRA, low rank adaptation, fine tunes a model by freezing the pretrained weight matrix W zero and learning an update as the product of two small matrices, B and A. B has the same number of rows as W and A the same number of columns, and they share a small inner dimension r, the rank, often around 4 to 8. In the forward pass I compute both terms and add them. For a 4,096 by 4,096 matrix, that's 16.8 million weights against 65 thousand with rank 8. Each task gets its own small A and B, so one base model serves many tasks.
must_mention: freeze W0, learn B times A
task specific A and B pairs

followups.q: How many parameters does LoRA train for a d by k matrix?
followups.a: r times d plus k, instead of d times k.

followups.q: Why can one base model serve many tasks?
followups.a: Each task only needs its own small A and B, which can be swapped in.

traps: Saying LoRA changes the pretrained weights. W0 stays frozen.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: Where should LoRA be applied, and what do we know about its learning rate, batch size and rank?
plain: The original LoRA paper trained only the attention matrices. Later work found that the feed forward blocks gain the most, so today both parts usually carry LoRA matrices. LoRA works best with a higher learning rate, about 10 times the usual one. One explanation is that the small matrices must explore a small space, so they need bigger steps. It also does worse with large batch sizes, and the reasons are only guesses so far. The rank r is a design choice, and a common value is 4. You can search over ranks, but the cut in size is already so large that the exact rank matters less. For example, if full fine tuning uses a learning rate of 0.00001, LoRA might use about 0.0001.
deep:
Placement: the original paper only trained the attention matrices. People later realized this is not where it helps most. A blog post from a few weeks before the lecture studied this in detail and found the feed forward blocks are where LoRA is most beneficial. Today both attention and feed forward blocks typically carry LoRA matrices, with most of the improvement coming from the feed forward block.

Two empirical properties (guidance from people who studied it, with no clean theory):

- Use a higher learning rate, typically around 10 times larger. A tentative reason: the rank is small, so given the small regions of space to explore, you need a higher learning rate.
- It performs worse with larger batch sizes. The hypothesis: the training dynamics of a product of matrices differ from those of a full matrix.

Rank: a design choice. You could grid search it, but people have done it before, so you can pick a popular value (4 is common). The initial reduction in parameters is orders of magnitude, so shrinking the rank further matters little. Other efficient tuning methods, prefix tuning and adapters, are explained in the textbook and less used.
say: The original paper applied LoRA to the attention matrices only, but later work found the feed forward blocks benefit most, so today both usually get adapters. Empirically, LoRA wants a higher learning rate, around ten times the full fine tuning value, and it does worse with large batch sizes. The explanations are tentative: a small rank means a small region to explore, so a higher learning rate helps, and the dynamics of a product of matrices differ from a full matrix. The rank itself is a design choice. Four is common, and you can search, but the size reduction is already so large that the exact rank matters less.
must_mention: originally attention only, now feed forward too
feed forward gives most of the gain
rank is a design choice, 4 is common

followups.q: Where does LoRA help most?
followups.a: In the feed forward blocks, though both attention and feed forward usually carry it today.

followups.q: What learning rate guidance applies?
followups.a: Around ten times the learning rate you would use for full fine tuning.

traps: Using the same learning rate and a huge batch size as for full fine tuning.

topic: CME295 L4: LLM training
q: What is QLoRA, and what are NF4 and double quantization?
plain: Quantized low rank adaptation (QLoRA) trains LoRA matrices on top of a base model stored in 4 bits. The small A and B matrices stay in a 16 bit format called BF16 (brain float 16). The 4 bit format is called NF4, short for normal float 4. NF4 assumes weights follow a bell shaped normal distribution. It places its 16 levels at quantiles, so each level covers about the same number of weights. Double quantization then compresses the scaling constants used for the conversion. Together they let a big model be tuned on far less memory. For example, 7 billion weights take 14 gigabytes at 16 bits but about 3.5 gigabytes at 4 bits.
deep:
QLoRA combines quantization with LoRA: quantize the frozen weights $W_0$ into a very compact format, and learn $A$ and $B$ in full precision (BF16 in the paper). The forward pass converts quantized blocks back on the fly (standard background).

NF4 (normal float 4): the format assumes weights are normally distributed. Instead of buckets of fixed size, it splits the space into quantiles of that distribution, so each bucket holds about the same number of values. This optimizes the use of the 16 levels that 4 bits can encode. (Equal probability levels for a standard normal have midpoints near $\pm0.08,\pm0.24,\dots,\pm1.86$, which is my own illustration of the idea; the real NF4 table is a fixed set of 16 values.)

Double quantization: converting weights in and out of the quantized state needs constants, and these constants are themselves quantized. The lecture says the first step gives large memory (VRAM) savings and the second gives extra savings that are smaller but still interesting. Arithmetic for weights alone: $7\times10^9\times2$ bytes $=14$ GB in 16 bits against $7\times10^9\times0.5=3.5$ GB in 4 bits, a 4 times reduction. (The slide's exact savings figure was unclear in the captions, so I do not quote it.)
say: QLoRA, quantized LoRA, puts LoRA on top of a base model whose frozen weights are stored in four bits, while the small A and B matrices stay in higher precision, BF16. The four bit format is NF4, which assumes the weights follow a normal distribution and places its quantization levels at quantiles, so each level covers about the same number of weights. Double quantization then quantizes the scaling constants used to convert in and out of the quantized state. Together they cut memory a lot: seven billion weights take about 14 gigabytes in 16 bits but about 3.5 in 4 bits.
must_mention: A and B stay in BF16

followups.q: Why quantiles instead of equal width buckets?
followups.a: Normally distributed weights cluster near zero, so quantile buckets give each level the same number of weights and use the bits better.

followups.q: What is double quantization?
followups.a: Quantizing the quantization constants themselves for a little more memory saving.

topic: CME295 L5: Preference tuning, RLHF and DPO
q: Why do we need preference tuning after SFT?
plain: SFT teaches a model what to say, but preference tuning teaches it which of two answers people prefer. Writing an ideal answer from scratch is hard, but picking the better of two answers is easy. SFT prompts must be balanced carefully, because too many of one kind bias the model. Fixing each misbehavior by adding an SFT example is slow, since every example must be high quality. Preference tuning also gives a negative signal, telling the model what not to produce. SFT only shows what to predict, never what to avoid. If an SFT model misbehaves a lot, first check the SFT data for problems. For example, 2 answers with the same facts can differ in tone, and preference tuning favors the friendlier one.
deep:
Pipeline so far: pretraining (language and code), then supervised fine tuning (SFT, a smaller, much higher quality dataset that teaches behavior). Preference tuning is the third step: align the SFT model with human preferences, for example when an assistant behaves correctly but not in the tone you want (not friendly, or not safe).

Reasons for a third step (lecture):

1. Cheaper data: building the ideal outputs for SFT is time consuming and difficult. It is much easier to show two answers and ask which is better, like comparing a bad poem and a great poem instead of writing a great poem from scratch.
2. Prompt distribution: SFT data needs a carefully balanced distribution of prompts, since too much of one kind biases the model. Adding a single example to fix a misbehavior risks biasing the model in that direction.
3. Cost of high quality data: chasing every misstep of the model with new SFT data takes a lot of time. If SFT misbehaves a lot, the SFT dataset itself may have a problem, so check it first, because preference tuning is not the answer to everything.
4. Negative signal: SFT teaches what the model should predict but not what it should not predict. Preference tuning can inject negative signal.

Relation to LoRA (Q and A): LoRA reduces the number of parameters you tune, while preference tuning is a different objective function, so the two are not incompatible.
say: SFT teaches the model what to produce, but preference tuning teaches it which answer people prefer, and I'd give four reasons for adding it. First, it's much easier to label which of two answers is better than to write a perfect one from scratch. Second, SFT data has to be balanced carefully, and adding one example to fix a behavior can bias the model. Third, curated SFT data is expensive. Fourth, preference tuning gives a negative signal, telling the model what not to generate, which SFT can't. But if the SFT model misbehaves a lot, I'd check the SFT data first, since preference tuning isn't the answer to everything.
must_mention: comparing is easier than writing ideal answers
SFT prompt distribution must stay balanced
SFT data is expensive to chase
negative signal: what not to generate

followups.q: What can SFT not express?
followups.a: What the model should avoid generating, unless you rewrite the bad output into a perfect one.

followups.q: Is preference tuning a replacement for LoRA?
followups.a: No. LoRA reduces how many parameters are tuned, while preference tuning changes the objective, and they can be combined.

traps: Treating preference tuning as the fix for any bad behavior instead of checking the SFT data.

topic: CME295 L5: Preference tuning, RLHF and DPO
q: What are the ways to collect preference data, and which one is used?
plain: Preference data says which responses people like, and it can be collected in three ways. Pointwise data gives each response its own score, which is hard because it is unclear how to scale scores. Pairwise data shows two responses and asks which one is better, which is much easier. Listwise data asks for a full ranking of several responses, which is easier than scores but still more work. Most teams use pairwise data, usually with just a better or worse label. Each training example is a prompt, a chosen response and a rejected response. For example, 50,000 prompts with 2 responses each give 50,000 preference pairs.
deep:
Setup: a prompt such as write a poem and a model response. Three ways to build preference data:

- Pointwise: score each proposed response on its own. Hard for a human, since it is not clear how to scale it (is this one 0.9 and that one 0.2?).
- Pairwise: look at two observations at a time and say which is better. Much easier.
- Listwise: get a list of $n$ responses and rank them, best to worst. Easier than pointwise because you need not say how much better, but still more complicated than a pair.

People typically use pairwise data: for each prompt there are two answers and a label saying which one is better. Notation used afterwards: a winning response $y_w$ and a losing response $y_l$, so each example is $(x,y_w,y_l)$.
say: There are three ways to collect preference data. Pointwise gives each response its own score, but humans find it hard to say whether something is a 0.9 or a 0.2, and the scale is unclear. Pairwise shows two responses and asks which is better, which is much easier. Listwise asks for a ranking of several responses, which avoids scores but is still more work than a pair. In practice most teams use pairwise data, usually with a simple better or worse label, so each example is a prompt with a chosen and a rejected response.
must_mention: pointwise: one score per response, hard to scale
pairwise: which of two is better

followups.q: Why is pointwise scoring hard for humans?
followups.a: It is not clear how to scale scores, so ratings are inconsistent.

followups.q: What does one pairwise example contain?
followups.a: A prompt, a winning response and a losing response.

traps: Thinking preference data needs absolute quality scores.

topic: CME295 L5: Preference tuning, RLHF and DPO
q: How is pairwise preference data created in practice?
plain: First pick a prompt that matches what real users ask, for example from product logs. Then run the model twice with a temperature above 0, so the two answers differ. Next, decide which answer is better, using human raters or a large language model (LLM) as a judge. The label is usually binary, better or worse, because finer scales are subjective. Another route is to take a disliked answer from the logs and rewrite it into a good one. Rewriting costs more, because writing is harder than comparing. For example, 2 samples at temperature 1 for each of 10,000 prompts give 10,000 pairs to rate.
deep:
Recipe:

1. Pick a prompt $x$ that follows the distribution of what users typically ask (from the logs, or from a desired set of prompts).
2. Run the prompt through the model twice with a positive temperature (Lecture 3), to obtain two different completions.
3. Compare them. Options: human ratings, an LLM as a judge (Lecture 8), or rule based metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE (less used now).
4. Choose a scale. The simplest is binary (is response 1 better or worse than response 2). A nuanced scale (much better, better, slightly better, slightly worse, worse, much worse) is possible, but many tasks are subjective, so a binary pairwise dataset is common.

Alternative: find in your logs a response you did not like and rewrite it into a good one, producing a pair (the lecture's teddy bear example). It is more involved because generation is costly.

Prompt choice matters: following the real user distribution keeps the tuning relevant.
say: To create pairwise data, I take prompts that match what real users ask, often from logs, and run the model twice at a positive temperature so the two answers differ. Then I decide which is better, using human raters, an LLM as a judge, or less often rule based scores like BLEU and ROUGE. The label is usually binary, because finer scales like much better or slightly better are subjective. Another route is to find an answer I disliked in the logs and rewrite it into a good one, which gives a pair but costs more, since writing is harder than comparing.
must_mention: prompts that follow real user traffic
rate with humans or an LLM judge
rewriting a disliked answer is another route

followups.q: Why sample at a positive temperature?
followups.a: At temperature 0 both runs would give the same answer, so there would be no pair to compare.

followups.q: Why use binary labels?
followups.a: Finer scales are subjective, so binary better or worse labels are more consistent.

traps: Using only temperature 0 samples, which makes identical pairs.

topic: CME295 L5: Preference tuning, RLHF and DPO
q: How do reinforcement learning ideas map onto an LLM, and why is the reward signal sparse?
plain: In reinforcement learning (RL), an agent in a state takes an action, follows a policy and receives a reward. The policy is the probability of each action given the state. For an LLM, the state is the text so far and the action is the next token. The policy is the model's probability distribution over the next token. The reward comes from a score for the whole completion, not for each token. So the signal is sparse, with about one reward per response. SFT gives a learning signal at every token, so RL gets much less information per example. For example, a 200 token answer gets 200 training signals in SFT, but only 1 reward in RL.
deep:
RL vocabulary: an agent interacts with an environment. At time $t$ it is in state $s_t$, takes action $a_t$ according to a policy $\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)$ (the probability of taking an action given the state), and receives a reward.

Transposed to an LLM:

| RL term | LLM meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Agent | the LLM |
| State $s_t$ | the input so far (prompt plus tokens generated so far) |
| Action $a_t$ | the next token, drawn from the vocabulary |
| Policy $\pi_\theta$ | the output probability distribution of the LLM for the next token |
| Reward | a score derived from the preference data, fed back into tuning |

The reward is given for the whole completion, not per token (Q and A), so RLHF is seen as an approach with a sparse signal: roughly one signal per completion, against SFT where every partial input trains the next token prediction. This is one reason RL tuning is harder than SFT. The cost per step is not special: you train in batches like other procedures, with extra parts that the next cards describe.
say: In reinforcement learning an agent, in some state, takes an action according to a policy and gets a reward. For an LLM, the agent is the model, the state is the text so far, the action is the next token, and the policy is the output probability distribution over the vocabulary. The reward comes from scoring the whole completion, not each token, so the signal is sparse: roughly one number per response, compared with a training signal at every token in SFT. That sparsity is one reason RLHF is harder to train than supervised methods.
must_mention: state is the input so far

followups.q: Is the reward given per token?
followups.a: No. It is given for the whole completion, which is why the signal is sparse.

followups.q: What plays the role of the environment?
followups.a: The set of tokens in the vocabulary that the model chooses from.

traps: Saying the reward is computed token by token.

topic: CME295 L5: Preference tuning, RLHF and DPO
q: What is RLHF, and what are its two stages?
plain: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aligns a model in two stages. Stage one trains a reward model, which takes a prompt and a response and outputs a score. Stage two uses reinforcement learning to tune the language model so its answers earn higher scores. The human feedback is the set of labels the reward model learns from. If the labels come from an AI instead of people, the method is called RLAIF (reinforcement learning from AI feedback). The goal is to find model weights so that the model's policy matches the preferences. For example, 1 reward model trained on 50,000 pairs can then score 100,000 or more prompts in stage two.
deep:
Goal: learn $\theta$, the LLM parameters, such that the policy $\pi_\theta$ aligns with preferences.

RLHF has two stages:

1. Learn to distinguish good outputs from bad ones. The preference pairs are used to train a reward model whose input is the concatenation of the prompt and a response and whose output is a score.
2. The RL step: use the rewards to align the model. The input is a prompt, and the LLM learns to generate $\hat y$ with higher reward.

The human feedback in RLHF refers to the labels on which the reward model is trained. If the preference pairs come from human ratings, it is RLHF. If they come from non human preferences it is RLAIF (reinforcement learning from AI feedback).

Orders of magnitude (later cards): tens of thousands of labeled pairs or more for the reward model, and at least 100 thousand observations in the RL stage.
say: RLHF has two stages. In stage one I train a reward model that takes a prompt and a response and outputs a score, using preference pairs. In stage two I use reinforcement learning to tune the language model so its responses earn higher scores from that frozen reward model. The human feedback part refers to the labels the reward model learns from. If the preferences come from an AI instead, it's called RLAIF. Typically the reward model needs tens of thousands of labeled pairs and the RL stage uses at least a hundred thousand prompts.
must_mention: stage one: reward model from preference pairs
stage two: RL against the reward model
goal is a policy matching preferences

followups.q: What does the human in RLHF refer to?
followups.a: The labels used to train the reward model.

followups.q: What replaces humans in RLAIF?
followups.a: An AI model that gives the preference labels.

traps: Saying humans score every response during the RL stage. The frozen reward model does that.

topic: CME295 L5: Preference tuning, RLHF and DPO
q: What is the Bradley Terry model, and how does it relate two reward scores to a preference?
plain: The Bradley Terry model turns two reward scores into the chance that one response beats the other. That chance is the sigmoid (a curve that maps any number to between 0 and 1) of the score difference. If response i scores much higher than response j, the difference is large and the chance is near 1. If both score the same, the difference is 0 and the chance is exactly 0.5. Training pushes the winner's score up and the loser's score down, so the chances match the human labels. Only the difference of scores matters, not their absolute size. For example, scores 2 and 0 give a chance of about 0.88 that the first wins.
deep:
$$
P(y_i\succ y_j)=\frac{e^{r_i}}{e^{r_i}+e^{r_j}}=\sigma(r_i-r_j),\qquad \sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}
$$

The second form follows by dividing numerator and denominator by $e^{r_i}$. The sigmoid goes to 0 at minus infinity and to 1 at plus infinity, so if $y_i$ is better than $y_j$ you want $r_i-r_j$ as high as possible, with $r_i$ high for good outputs and $r_j$ low for bad ones.

Because it uses a pairwise dataset, the formulation has two scores, one per response. It is invariant to adding the same constant to every score, so only differences matter.

Check: $r_i=2$, $r_j=0$ gives $\sigma(2)=0.881$. Equal scores give $\sigma(0)=0.5$.
say: The Bradley Terry model says the probability that response i beats response j is e to the r i divided by e to the r i plus e to the r j, which equals the sigmoid of r i minus r j. So only the score difference matters. If i scores much higher, the sigmoid is near one, and if the scores are equal, it's one half. For example, scores of two and zero give about 0.88.
